This suggests that SMA pathogenesis could be widespread throughout the central nervous system. The use of antisense oligonucleotides targeting SMN expression in the early stages of organoid development showed a rescue of both morphological and functional deficits in SMA spinal cord organoids. Erroneous splicing in SMN1-target mRNAs was corrected by early treatment.
Overall the manuscript provides important insights into early pathogenesis mechanisms of SMA, which could not be easily assessed without using human iPS cell-derived neural organoids. The comparison between “spinal cord” and “cerebral” organoids could highlight similarity and difference of the disease-induced alterations. Antisense oligonucleotide treatment of organoids demonstrated treatment mechanisms at cellular and molecular levels. The manuscript gives important insights into SMA pathophysiology and disease modeling methodology. However, I have concerns and comments on the manuscript as below.
Comments:
The “spinal cord organoids” are characterized by immnunostaining and scRNAseq. Please compare percent of key cell types (motorneurons, inhibitory neurons, excitatory neurons, progenitors, glia etc) observed by immnunostaning and scRNAseq so that the cellular composition of the organoids.
Comparison of the cellular composition between spinal cord organoids and cerebral organoids is critical as basis for the overall study.
Please include HB9 for identification of motor neurons.
Retinoic acid-induced ventralization could reduce other types of cells in the organoids. Please discuss how retinoid acid-mediated differentiation was controlled in the spinal organoids. Figure 4a indicates SAG and RA are always added to the culture media. Was this intended to maximize motor neuron differentiation and maintenance?
Figure 3d indicated reduction of axon length in SMA neurons from spinal cord organoids. Was this similar in neurons from cerebral organoids?
Please explain the y-axis of Figure 4d in more detail. Was it “increased” percentage from the base line? Was it measured right after adding glutamate directly onto the organoids? Please also provide representative traces and raster plots.
Also was Extended Figure 10i analyzed at similar time point with Figure 4d? Representative traces should be presented to know temporal changes.
Was active number of electrodes different between SMA, control organoids, and MO-treated SMA organoids?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this study, the authors use control and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) spinal cord and cerebral organoids to examine the evolution of gene expression abnormalities over developmental time using single cell sequencing and to assess changes in pre-mRNA splicing patterns after treated with a splice switching antisense oligonucleotide. Emerging data indicate that SMA may start in utero with developmental impairments that are associated with vulnerability to rapid degeneration. Understanding the molecular events underlying these developmental and degenerative events are key for understanding how to optimize therapy.
The major findings of this study are 1) SMA spinal cord organoids may be a useful model of human SMA in vitro 2) there are histological and gene expression signatures suggesting very early developmental slowing involving neuronal and nonneuronal cells and 3) a small proportion of abnormal splicing events improve with ASO treatment. Important strengths of the paper are the effort to develop a human SMA spinal organoid model as prior attempts to look at 2D iPSC derived MNs have not clearly revealed disease relevant pathologies. Further the detailed sequencing of human cells has the potential to reveal new insights into disease pathogenesis. Unfortunately, in its current form, there are several experimental limitations (see below. Although the observation of developmental slowing is interesting, it is not clear whether these findings are relevant for the human disease and there is no mechanistic investigation of the identified gene expression changes to validate their importance.
Specific comments:
1) Several aspects of the initial CNTL and SMA organoid characterizations need to be strengthed. In an extended table, 6 CNTL and 7 SMA lines are listed ranging in age from newborn to 34 years for CNTL and fetal to 2 years for SMA. Only some of these lines are actually used in the paper and for most experiments only 1 to 2 lines each are used. It must be clarified which lines are used for which experiments and whether the differences in subject age play an important role in the behavior of the iPSCs. Further, a minium of 3 lines each (with duplicate derivations) should be used for most experiments. No information regarding SMN1/SMN2 copy number or SMA type is provided. There is no baseline assessment of SMN mRNA or protein levels amongst the different lines over differentiation time (the authors make the point in the intro that SMN may decrease in whole human tissues over developmental time). Although key markers of iPSC differentiation are quantified over differentiation time in several CNTL lines, this quantitative data are not provided for the SMA lines (Ext data figure 1).
2) During the initial characterization of the SMA organoids, the authors note a transcription profile that correlates with Carnegie Stage CS17. They refer to this as a human fetal stage, but in fact this classifcation refers to human embryo staging (first 10 weeks of gestation are embyro and 10-40 weeks are fetus). This is an important distinction as this implies that the organoids are VERY IMMATURE. Although studies of human type I SMA tissues indicate MN developmental abnormalities at mid-late fetal stages, I am not aware of abnormalities dating to the embyro. How do the authors conceptualize the developmental processes in these organoids relative to human SMA development.
3) There seems to be a disconnect between the number of SOX2+ neural progenitors at 1 month and 2 month (CNTL and SMA are equivalent at 2 months) compared to the number of apoptotic cells at these same time points. The authors need to provide the statistical comparison between CNTL and SMA in number of apoptotic cells at 1 mo and 2 months. What cell types are actually dying at 2 months? Do MNs actually undergo apoptotic cells death or is this another cell type?
4) The authors note that there are many gene expression abnormalities between SMA and CNTL, but identify only one gene (NRXN2) that has been previously reported to be altered in SMA tissue. A formal comparison to other data sets might help strengthen the relevance of these gene expression changes.
5) SMI32 is used to define axon length. More thorough analysis to prove these are MNs with MN specific markers and stains that would specifically identify axons vs. dendrites. As is perhaps more accurate to call neurites?
6) Extended data 9 includes only 1 CNTL line (see comment about n above).
7) There is inadequate characterization of the cerebral oraganoids with no quantification of the basic markers over differentation time. Very similar histological and electrophysiological phentoypes are reported in these organoids as reported in the SC organoids. Although the brain may be affected in some very severely affected SMA patients, it is much less severely affected than the spinal cord. It would have been much more impactful to see divergent phenotypes between these two organoid systems-why is this not seen?
9) The treatment experiments as currently presented are not sufficiently rigorous. CNTL lines need to be run in parallel to assess nonspecific changes arising from treatment and as a reference point for SMN expression. A scrambled ASO is also needed. The targeting of the ASO to cells in these organoids need to directly assessed. How many cells and what cell types actually took up the ASO? Were the modest improvements in splicing patterns due to inadequate drug distribution or splicing changes no longer reversible by SMN induction? Those genes that can not reverse their splicing pattern even after full SMN repletion would be very interesting for the SMA field to identify particularly if they are relevant to disease manifestations in patients.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We thank the Reviewers for their enthusiasm for our work and for their thoughtful comments and constructive feedback for the revisions. We have now addressed all the comments through extensive new data and analyses, as well as text revisions. Here, we first highlight the major changes to the revised manuscript and then address each of the Reviewers' comments point-by-point.
• We have profiled the iPSC lines generated de novo for this publication and specified the features of the commercial and previously published lines. This sums up to 5 iPSC patient and control lines on which most of our analyses have been conducted. This resulted in a new supplementary figure and a new supplementary table (Extended (Ext.) Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1).
• We have generated extensive new data on brain organoids showing a robust functional phenotype, but not a difference in the general amount of SOX2 positive progenitors at the analyzed time point (Fig. 4 and Ext. Data Fig. 9). Our study therefore proposes, for the first time, a direct investigation of brain SMA phenotype and highlights an important difference between brain and spinal cord organoids in the context of SMA pathogenesis.
• As requested, we have increased the number of biological replicates and revised all the immunostaining panels and relative quantification for clarity, adding a color code system to specify which lines were used for each analysis.
• We have also extended our results with numerous new analyses to further support our findings: we added new electrophysiological replicates to all the functional analyses, we updated our single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets with novel computational tools, and we added novel computational analyses for the developmental trajectory and splicing activity.
• We also included novel experiments demonstrating the splicing alternative patterns induced by SMA alterations and rescued by the antisense oligonucleotide treatment. We leveraged a customized scramble sequence to further validate our results, and we repeated all the experiments. In addition, to address the biodistribution pattern of the ASO treatment, we employed a customized biotinylated ASO sequence and verified the extent of the treatment distribution in spinal cord organoids.
Overall, with the addition of these data and analyses, we are confident that we have addressed all the points raised by the Reviewers. These data further reinforce our conclusions on progenitor involvement in the pathology and the pervasive cellular response to a clinically meaningful molecular treatment.
We address the Reviewers' specific comments below.

We have carefully considered the Reviewer’s suggestions regarding human iPSC characterization and have made substantial changes to the data visualization and analysis. These valuable suggestions from the Reviewer have significantly strengthened the quality of our work.

We thank the Reviewer for highlighting this important point regarding statistical power and the reproducibility of our results across batches and lines. To address this, we have now provided color-coded graphs where organoids are annotated by their cell line of origin. These visualizations demonstrate that multiple replicates and cell lines were analyzed throughout the study, with negligible inter-line effects observed.
As part of this revision, we increased the number of replicates and batches for each cell line to further strengthen the robustness of our analyses. These updates are detailed in the newly generated Supplementary Table 1 and are reflected across all relevant figures in the revised manuscript.

We agree with the Reviewer that the rationale for our previous annotation was not extensively described in the main text and was only briefly mentioned in the Materials and Methods section. For the annotation, we used marker genes and confirmed their cell type specificity using the human spinal cord atlas published by Rayon et al., (2021) as a reference (PMID: 34351410).
We wish to thank the Reviewer for their valuable suggestion, which we have now analyzed and incorporated into our comparison. Specifically, we have included a comprehensive panel listing all the markers from the reference cited by the Reviewer, as well as the most important genes used to annotate the clusters. Furthermore, we expanded our list of annotated genes to 300, which is now provided in the revised Supplementary Table 4.
Comment 4
Most of the immunofluorescence images are below an acceptable quality and fail to properly represent quantitative data or prove co-localization of protein expression, thus hampering proper characterization. For instance: 1) SOX2 staining in Figure 2a SMA panel seems to show increased positive cells in the patients compared to control, or unspecific staining; 2) Figure 2c does not show an increased TUJ1 positivity in the SMA patient SCOs; 3) in Figure 3d is not clear what has been measured to quantify the neurites length, neither proper information is given in the figure legends; 4) Extended Figure 5a is not proving any positivity for TUNEL analysis, while it mostly shows unspecific and spatial restricted signal, which might lead to bias in the interpretation (how quantification has been taken?); Extended Figure 9c immunofluorescence for GAD65 is not really showing believable neurons, and control and SMA images seems at different magnification.
We thank the Reviewer for raising these important concerns, and we apologize for the previously low-quality images, which resulted from erroneous file compression during the submission process. To address these issues, we have reorganized and replaced the affected figures with higher-quality images that include appropriate magnifications to enhance clarity and accurately represent the phenotypes.
SOX2 and TUJ1 Staining (Fig 2a, b): we have replaced these images with higher-quality, more representative versions that clearly illustrate the differences in SOX2-positive and TUJ1-positive cells between SMA and control SCOs. These improvements significantly reduce the likelihood of misinterpretation and better convey the findings described in our study.
Neurite Length Quantification (Fig. 3h): we have clarified the method used to quantify neurite length in the revised manuscript methods.
TUNEL Staining (Fig. 5d and Ext. Data Fig. 5a): recognizing the Reviewer’s concerns about the spatially restricted signal and potential bias in interpretation, we have included new representative images that more clearly demonstrate how TUNEL quantification was conducted. This provides a more accurate representation of our analyses and supports the conclusions presented.
GAD65 Immunofluorescence (Ext. Data Fig. 8b): we replaced the images for GAD65 with higher-quality visuals that distinctly show neuronal populations. To further corroborate our findings, we also performed additional staining for GABA, which is now included in the revised manuscript. These additions provide more robust evidence supporting our interpretations.
We believe that these revisions, informed by the Reviewer’s constructive feedback, have significantly improved the quality and clarity of the immunofluorescence data presented in our study. These updated figures and explanations are now included in the revised manuscript.
Comment 5
Some of the conclusion in the results section do not appear properly justified by the data provided. For instance, page 7 lines 208-217, the solely use of the TUNEL technique does not allow conclusion of cellular death process. Beside the not convincing representative immunofluorescence analysis (see Comment 4), other analysis should have been provided to identify the population undergoing cell death (motor neurons, progenitors, other neurons?). We appreciate the Reviewer’s suggestion to conduct additional analyses to confirm cell death processes. While we attempted supplementary staining with markers such as caspase-3, these efforts unfortunately did not yield reliable results. Additionally, we encountered technical limitations commonly associated with three-dimensional organoid systems due to the presence of the extracellular matrix. These limitations hindered our attempts to perform double staining of TUNEL with other markers, as the harsh conditions required for the TUNEL protocol interfered with other staining procedures. We have acknowledged these limitations in the manuscript and have tempered our conclusions regarding cell death accordingly.
To strengthen our findings, we leveraged scRNA-seq data to investigate the enrichment of apoptotic genes. Our analyses revealed that the motor neuron cluster exhibited the highest enrichment for apoptotic gene ontology terms among the relevant clusters (Ext. Data Fig. 5c). This finding highlights the specific vulnerability of motor neurons to apoptotic processes, even if indirectly.

The Reviewer raises an important point, and we thank them for highlighting this. To clarify, we increased the number of replicates for the analyses and conducted a longitudinal study to strengthen the findings and ensure consistency.
In CTRL SCOs, we observed a clear reduction in SOX2-expressing neural progenitors and a corresponding increase in the post-mitotic neuronal marker TUJ1 between 1 and 2 months. In contrast, SMA SCOs exhibited a less pronounced reduction in SOX2 and no significant increase in TUJ1-positive cells over the same period (revised Fig. 2a-d). In the scRNA-seq analysis of the 2-month dataset, the trajectory revealed two primary branches. One branch contained progenitors in distinct proliferative states and committed progenitors of the floor plate, while the other branch comprised neural progenitors progressing toward differentiated neurons (revised Fig. 2e-g). SMA SCOs showed a markedly different distribution of cell states compared to CTRL SCOs, with an increased representation of cells at the starting and early segments of the developmental trajectory, indicative of an intermediate stage of development. This altered trajectory was accompanied by a robust and statistically significant reduction in cells reaching the endpoint of the trajectory, which represents maturing neuronal subtypes.
Altogether, these findings reflect the developmental delay and altered trajectory in SMA SCOs, where progenitors remain abundant, but progression to terminally differentiated neurons is impaired. We believe these integrated analyses provide a clearer picture of the phenotypic differences in SMA SCOs and have clarified this in the revised manuscript.
Comment 7
Page 13 line 398 the conclusion that unconjugated MO does not rescue phenotype due to increased organoids size is not demonstrated. Testing in smaller organoids should be provided. Moreover, this set of experiments should have included a scrambled oligonucleotide to side to untreated.
In response to the Reviewer’s concern regarding the impact of organoid size on phenotype rescue, we confirm that organoids of similar sizes were used throughout molecular profiling experiments to minimize size-related variability. The Reviewer raises an important point regarding the biodistribution of the treatment: to address this, we conjugated morpholino oligonucleotide (MO) with biotin, enabling us to assess its perfusion (Ext. Data Fig. 10). Our analyses revealed effective MO distribution reaching the center of medium-to-large organoids (approximately 3.5 mm in diameter), suggesting adequate delivery of the treatment in these experiments.
While we did not include a scrambled MO in the specific phenotypic assays due to the large quantity of MO required, we did utilize a scrambled MO in our molecular comparisons and splicing analyses (Ext. Data Fig. 10-11). This provided a stringent control framework for evaluating the specificity of MO-mediated effects, strengthening the conclusions of our study. We have clarified these points in the revised manuscript to address the Reviewer’s concerns.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study, Faravelli et al compared human SMA type 1 “spinal cord organoids” and “cerebral organoids” from multiple donors. Single-cell RNA-seq revealed changes in the gene expression in various cell types, not only in motor neurons. These included neural progenitors and showed pathological changes in neuronal differentiation. Multi-electrode array analysis showed abnormalities in the activity of both SMA spinal and cerebral organoids. This suggests that SMA pathogenesis could be widespread throughout the central nervous system. The use of antisense oligonucleotides targeting SMN expression in the early stages of organoid development showed a rescue of both morphological and functional deficits in SMA spinal cord organoids. Erroneous splicing in SMN1-target mRNAs was corrected by early treatment.
Overall the manuscript provides important insights into early pathogenesis mechanisms of SMA, which could not be easily assessed without using human iPS cell-derived neural organoids. The comparison between “spinal cord” and “cerebral” organoids highlighting similarities and differences in disease-induced alterations, as well as the demonstration of treatment mechanisms at cellular and molecular levels, are indeed novel valuable contributions to the field. The suggestions to strengthen the study design and the depth of the analysis were valuable and have improved our manuscript. Below, we detail our point-by-point response to each suggestion, and we believe we have comprehensively addressed the Reviewer’s concerns, providing further support for our results, and highlighting the overall value of the study.
Comment
The “spinal cord organoids” are characterized by immnunostaining and scRNAseq. Please compare percent of key cell types (motorneurons, inhibitory neurons, excitatory neurons, progenitors, glia etc) observed by immnunostaning and scRNAseq so that the cellular composition of the organoids. Comparison of the cellular composition between spinal cord organoids and cerebral organoids is critical as basis for the overall study. Please include HB9 for identification of motor neurons.
We wish to thank the Reviewer for their kind remarks regarding the significance of our work in the field of SMA. In response to their comments, we have conducted additional analyses using both immunostaining and scRNA-seq data to provide a comprehensive characterization of the cellular composition of spinal cord organoids and facilitate a robust comparison with cerebral organoids.
To specifically address the identification of motor neurons, we included HB9 immunostaining using a customized and validated antibody obtained in collaboration with the Motor Neuron Center at Columbia University. Additionally, we performed longitudinal immunostaining for SOX2 (progenitor marker) and TUJ1 (neuronal marker). To improve the robustness of these analyses, we increased the number of replicates and provided novel high-resolution immunostaining panels in the revised manuscript. These updates further highlight key differences between CTRL and SMA spinal cord organoids. Specifically, CTRL organoids exhibited a clear reduction in SOX2-expressing neural progenitors and an increase in TUJ1-positive post-mitotic neurons between 1 and 2 months, while SMA organoids showed a less pronounced reduction in SOX2 levels and no significant increase in TUJ1-expressing cells, reflecting a developmental delay.
For cerebral organoids, we specifically assessed whether neural progenitors are affected in SMA by quantifying SOX2+ cells. Our results revealed no significant differences in SOX2+ cell populations between CTRL and SMA cerebral organoids. This finding supports a milder phenotype in the brain compared to the spinal cord, consistent with the known pathogenesis of SMA, where the spinal cord is typically more severely impacted.
ScRNA-seq analysis further validated these findings by revealing distinct cellular trajectories in the 2-month dataset. Cells in CTRL spinal cord organoids split into two primary branches: one comprising progenitors in different proliferative states and committed progenitors of the floor plate, and the other comprising progenitors differentiating into mature neuronal subtypes. In SMA spinal cord organoids, the distribution of cell states was significantly altered, with an increased representation of cells at earlier developmental stages and a statistically significant reduction in cells reaching the endpoint of the trajectory, corresponding to mature neurons (revised Fig. 2f-g).
To ensure robust comparisons of cellular composition, we reanalyzed the scRNA-seq data using the latest computational pipelines, allowing for a more accurate characterization of transcriptional differences. This included a detailed analysis of unmatched SMA cells and a partitioning of the scRNA-seq dataset to examine motor neuron lineages across pseudotime and differentiation stages. These additional insights, now included in the revised manuscript (new Fig. 3), strengthen the foundation of our study and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the cellular differences between SMA and CTRL organoids.
Retinoic acid-induced ventralization could reduce other types of cells in the organoids. Please discuss how retinoid acid-mediated differentiation was controlled in the spinal organoids. Figure 4a indicates SAG and RA are always added to the culture media. Was this intended to maximize motor neuron differentiation and maintenance?
To achieve a spinal organoid model with a high proportion of motor neurons, we employed a combination of retinoic acid (RA) and Smoothened Agonist (SAG). This approach was specifically designed to impart a rostral spinal cord identity to the organoids while simultaneously promoting ventralization, which is essential for motor neuron specification. The consistent addition of RA and SAG to the culture media was intended to maximize motor neuron differentiation and maintenance.
While this protocol prioritizes motor neuron production, it also supports the differentiation of spinal cord interneurons, providing a more comprehensive spinal cord-like cellular diversity. To mitigate potential over-ventralization effects, we carefully optimized the concentrations and timing of RA and SAG addition to achieve a balanced cellular composition.
Our approach aligns with the conditions described in Andersen et al., 2020 (PMID: 33333020), particularly those outlined in conditions 11 and 12, where similar concentrations of RA and SAG were used to drive motor neuron differentiation while preserving cellular diversity within spinal organoids.
Figure 3d indicated reduction of axon length in SMA neurons from spinal cord organoids. Was this similar in neurons from cerebral organoids?
We thank the Reviewer for this insightful question. While we were unable to assess axon length in neurons derived from cerebral organoids due to technical limitations, we instead focused on the assessment of neural progenitors in cerebral organoids to provide a comparative phenotype. This allowed us to explore potential differences between spinal cord and cerebral organoids in the context of SMA.
Please explain the y-axis of Figure 4d in more detail. Was it “increased” percentage from the base line? Was it measured right after adding glutamate directly onto the organoids? Please also provide representative traces and raster plots. Also was Extended Figure 10i analyzed at similar time point with Figure 4d? Representative traces should be presented to know temporal changes. as active number of electrodes different between SMA, control organoids, and MO-treated SMA organoids?
We thank the Reviewer for these important comments, which allowed us to further refine and enhance the robustness of our functional analyses, a key point of novelty in this manuscript. The y-axis of Fig. 4d represents the percentage change in basal firing frequency. This was calculated by comparing the average firing frequency in the last 10 minutes before glutamate addition with the interval between 5-15 minutes after glutamate addition. This information has now been clearly specified in the Methods section.
To provide a more comprehensive view, we have added raster plots for the four conditions (CTRL and SMA, before and after glutamate) to the panel, alongside representative traces. These additions offer better visualization of temporal changes in neuronal activity. Importantly, the number of electrodes considered for the analysis was consistent across all three groups (CTRL, SMA, and MO-treated SMA organoids), and this has been explicitly noted in the Methods.
Regarding the timing of the analyses, we confirm that Ext. Data Fig. 9f (previously named Ext. Fig. 10i) was assessed at a similar time point as Fig. 4c (previously named Fig. 4d), ensuring comparability. Additionally, we have increased the number of replicates for the functional analyses and included a color-coded assignment for each genetic background to increase clarity and reproducibility.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study, the authors use control and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) spinal cord and cerebral organoids to examine the evolution of gene expression abnormalities over developmental time using single cell sequencing and to assess changes in pre-mRNA splicing patterns after treated with a splice switching antisense oligonucleotide. Emerging data indicate that SMA may start in utero with developmental impairments that are associated with vulnerability to rapid degeneration. Understanding the molecular events underlying these developmental and degenerative events are key for understanding how to optimize therapy.
The major findings of this study are 1) SMA spinal cord organoids may be a useful model of human SMA in vitro 2) there are histological and gene expression signatures suggesting very early developmental slowing involving neuronal and nonneuronal cells and 3) a small proportion of abnormal splicing events improve with ASO treatment. Important strengths of the paper are the effort to develop a human SMA spinal organoid model as prior attempts to look at 2D iPSC derived MNs have not clearly revealed disease relevant pathologies. Further the detailed sequencing of human cells has the potential to reveal new insights into disease pathogenesis. Unfortunately, in its current form, there are several experimental limitations (see below. Although the observation of developmental slowing is interesting, it is not clear whether these findings are relevant for the human disease and there is no mechanistic investigation of the identified gene expression changes to validate their importance.
We are grateful to Reviewer #3 for recognizing the significant strengths of our work and its potential implications for advancing the understanding of SMA pathology. We also deeply value the constructive suggestions to refine our study design, which have enabled us to draw more robust and accurate conclusions. In response to their feedback, we have thoroughly addressed each concern and believe that these improvements have substantially enhanced the rigor and impact of our study.
Specific comments:
1) Several aspects of the initial CNTL and SMA organoid characterizations need to be strengthed. In an extended table, 6 CNTL and 7 SMA lines are listed ranging in age from newborn to 34 years for CNTL and fetal to 2 years for SMA. Only some of these lines are actually used in the paper and for most experiments only 1 to 2 lines each are used. It must be clarified which lines are used for which experiments and whether the differences in subject age play an important role in the behavior of the iPSCs. Further, a minium of 3 lines each (with duplicate derivations) should be used for most experiments. No information regarding SMN1/SMN2 copy number or SMA type is provided. There is no baseline assessment of SMN mRNA or protein levels amongst the different lines over differentiation time (the authors make the point in the intro that SMN may decrease in whole human tissues over developmental time). Although key markers of iPSC differentiation are quantified over differentiation time in several CNTL lines, this quantitative data are not provided for the SMA lines (Ext data figure 1).
In the current version of the manuscript, we addressed all the points raised here by the Reviewer, further strengthening the robustness of our results.
We increased the number of lines for the experiments and made clearer their allocation in the different analyses (we provide a novel Supplementary Table 1 where all experiments are clarified, and we maintained a color code for each line throughout the entire manuscript). This implied the generation of new batches of both spinal cord and brain organoids from CTRL and SMA lines. We have now provided color-coded graphs where organoids have been annotated by the cell line of origin. As it can be observed, several replicates and multiple cell lines have been analyzed throughout all the analyses with negligible inter-line effect. For this revision, we increased the number of replicates and batches for each line, as highlighted both in the newly generated Supplementary Table 1 and across all figures in the manuscript.
For SMN1/2 copy number, we have now provided an extensive characterization of all the iPSC lines generated de novo for this work, including evaluation of 1) morphology, 2) genome integrity, and 3) self-renewal markers (newly generated Ext. Data Fig. 1). We used the same parameters on representative commercial lines, as internal controls. Regarding the commercial and previously published lines, we provided more detailed information about their source and features.
Finally, we extensively characterized the SMN molecular phenotype of the iPSC lines (such as qPCR analyses on the copies of SMN and the evaluation of the expression of the ratio FL/D7 SMN and SMN expression levels over time in culture, Ext. Data Fig. 1d-f) and provided further details of the clinical phenotypes of each donor/patient (Ext. Data Fig. 1h).
Key markers of iPSC differentiation have been quantified over in SMA lines as well in the revised version of the manuscript (Ext. Data Fig. 1g).
2) During the initial characterization of the SMA organoids, the authors note a transcription profile that correlates with Carnegie Stage CS17. They refer to this as a human fetal stage, but in fact this classifcation refers to human embryo staging (first 10 weeks of gestation are embyro and 10-40 weeks are fetus). This is an important distinction as this implies that the organoids are VERY IMMATURE. Although studies of human type I SMA tissues indicate MN developmental abnormalities at mid-late fetal stages, I am not aware of abnormalities dating to the embyro. How do the authors conceptualize the developmental processes in these organoids relative to human SMA development.
We thank the Reviewer for raising this important point and apologize for any lack of clarity in the original submission. In the revised manuscript, we updated our references for the endogenous tissue (Ext. Data Fig. 3c) to include a study that performed single-cell RNA sequencing of human spinal cord cells across multiple time points during embryonic and fetal stages. Our dataset showed the strongest alignment with early developmental stages (first trimester), and we have amended our text accordingly. The transcriptional alterations observed in progenitors, which represent a significant novelty, align with the developmental nature of the model and provide valuable insights into the early events of human spinal cord neurogenesis.
3) There seems to be a disconnect between the number of SOX2+ neural progenitors at 1 month and 2 month (CNTL and SMA are equivalent at 2 months) compared to the number of apoptotic cells at these same time points. The authors need to provide the statistical comparison between CNTL and SMA in number of apoptotic cells at 1 mo and 2 months. What cell types are actually dying at 2 months? Do MNs actually undergo apoptotic cells death or is this another cell type?
We thank the Reviewer for the opportunity to clarify these points. While CTRL SCOs exhibited a clear reduction in SOX2-expressing neural progenitors and an increase in the post-mitotic neuronal marker TUJ1 from 1 to 2 months, SMA SCOs demonstrated a less pronounced reduction in SOX2 levels and no significant increase in the proportion of TUJ1-expressing cells. Single-cell trajectory analysis of the 2-month dataset revealed two major branches: one containing progenitors in distinct states of proliferative activity and committed progenitors of the floor plate, and another comprising neural progenitors progressing toward differentiated neurons (revised Fig. 2f-g). SMA SCOs displayed a strikingly altered distribution of cell states, with an increased representation of cells at the starting and early segments of the developmental trajectory—indicative of an intermediate stage of development. This altered trajectory was accompanied by a robust and statistically significant reduction in cells at the endpoint of the trajectory, corresponding to maturing neuronal subtypes.
We appreciate the Reviewer’s suggestion to conduct further analyses to confirm cell death processes. Although we attempted supplementary staining using markers such as caspase-3, these efforts did not yield reliable results. Additionally, technical limitations—commonly encountered in 3D organoid models due to the extracellular matrix— made it challenging to perform double staining of TUNEL with other markers. The harsh conditions required for the TUNEL protocol interfered with other staining procedures. We have acknowledged this limitation in the manuscript and tempered our conclusions regarding cell death accordingly.
To address this challenge, we leveraged single-cell data to investigate the enrichment of apoptotic genes. Our analyses revealed that the motor neuron cluster exhibited the highest enrichment for apoptotic gene ontology terms among the relevant clusters (Ext. Data Fig. 5c). This observation, combined with the altered developmental trajectory in SMA SCOs, suggests that the vulnerability of motor neurons to apoptosis could be linked to their disrupted progression through differentiation.
4) The authors note that there are many gene expression abnormalities between SMA and CNTL, but identify only one gene (NRXN2) that has been previously reported to be altered in SMA tissue. A formal comparison to other data sets might help strengthen the relevance of these gene expression changes.
After reanalyzing our data using the latest scRNA-seq pipeline, we obtained a cleaner and more robust dataset. We performed a de novo comparison of bulk RNA-seq data from in vitro differentiated SMA and CTRL human motor neurons (PMID: 30649277) with the scRNA-seq differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified in motor neurons. This updated analysis yielded an expanded list of previously reported genes, now totaling 24. These include CAMK2B, GRIA1, GRM4, NRXN1, PCDH7, PCDH10, PRKCG, PSD2, SCN2A, and SNAP91, many of which are associated with neuronal function and ion channel activity.
5) SMI32 is used to define axon length. More thorough analysis to prove these are MNs with MN specific markers and stains that would specifically identify axons vs. dendrites. As is perhaps more accurate to call neurites?
We agree with the Reviewer and have amended the text and figure legend accordingly.
6) Extended data 9 includes only 1 CNTL line (see comment about n above).
The Reviewer is correct in pointing out this limitation. In the current version of the manuscript, we have highlighted the contribution of each cell line to the respective analyses. While we were unable to increase replicates across all experiments for the brain organoids due to cost and time constraints, we prioritized increasing the number of lines, batches, and replicates for the key experiments. This ensured alignment with the approach used for the spinal cord organoids. Specifically, for the functional analyses, this effort resulted in the production and analysis of additional organoids for the MEA glutamate assay (Fig. 4h, i).
7) There is inadequate characterization of the cerebral organoids with no quantification of the basic markers over differentation time.
Brain organoids are inherently heterogeneous, and we specifically selected this model to provide an unbiased assessment of the potential impact of SMA on the CNS. This approach allowed us to investigate the broad effects of SMA without limiting our analysis to specific brain regions, thereby supporting the overarching hypothesis of our study. While this heterogeneity adds value by capturing a more comprehensive view of SMA pathology, it also presents challenges in organoid-to-organoid reproducibility.
To address this, we focused our quantitative analyses on the general progenitor marker SOX2, assessing its expression at both the protein and RNA levels. This decision aligns with our findings in spinal cord organoids, which represent a central focus of the manuscript. Furthermore, we characterized the emergence of specific neural markers at selected time points to provide additional insights into the differentiation timeline and cellular composition of the organoids.
Very similar histological and electrophysiological phentoypes are reported in these organoids as reported in the SC organoids. Although the brain may be affected in some very severely affected SMA patients, it is much less severely affected than the spinal cord. It would have been much more impactful to see divergent phenotypes between these two organoid systems-why is this not seen?
We appreciate the Reviewer’s observation regarding the phenotypic similarities between the cerebral and spinal cord organoids and the suggestion that divergent phenotypes would be more impactful. To address this, we expanded our analysis on cerebral organoids, focusing on the characterization of fundamental markers and, in particular, progenitor cell phenotypes.
Specifically, we assessed whether neural progenitors are affected in SMA cerebral organoids by quantifying SOX2+ cells. Our results revealed no significant differences in SOX2+ cell populations between CTRL and SMA cerebral organoids. This finding supports the Reviewer’s suggestion of a milder phenotype in the brain compared to the spinal cord, consistent with the known pathogenesis of SMA, where the spinal cord is typically more severely impacted.
9) The treatment experiments as currently presented are not sufficiently rigorous. CNTL lines need to be run in parallel to assess nonspecific changes arising from treatment and as a reference point for SMN expression. A scrambled ASO is also needed. The targeting of the ASO to cells in these organoids need to directly assessed. How many cells and what cell types actually took up the ASO? Were the modest improvements in splicing patterns due to inadequate drug distribution or splicing changes no longer reversible by SMN induction? Those genes that can not reverse their splicing pattern even after full SMN repletion would be very interesting for the SMA field to identify particularly if they are relevant to disease manifestations in patients.
We thank the Reviewer for highlighting this important aspect. During the revisions, we conducted additional batches of SCOs and implemented a robust experimental design to address the concerns raised. Treatments with r6-MO, scrambled r6-MO, and collections of untreated SMA SCOs were performed in parallel, allowing us to assess nonspecific changes and establish an appropriate reference point, as suggested by the Reviewer. The use of scrambled r6-MO as a control provided a stringent analytical framework, ensuring that the observed changes were specific to r6-MO treatment. This approach enabled the identification of a robust set of key genes whose splicing was reverted upon r6-MO treatment (revised Fig. 6). Importantly, genes that did not exhibit splicing reversion were linked to broader pathophysiological processes, suggesting systemic involvement beyond spinal cord pathology (new Suppl. Table 10).
To address the distribution of r6-MO within the organoids, we utilized a biotinylated version of r6-MO and traced its localization using biotin staining (Ext. Data Fig. 10d). The staining revealed widespread distribution of r6-MO, spanning both the periphery and the center of the organoids. This widespread distribution, coupled with the recovery of SMN levels (Ext. Data Figure 10e), suggests that the modest splicing improvements observed are likely related to the irreversible splicing state of certain genes. Interestingly, among the genes associated with reverted splicing events, we identified histone-modifying enzymes, which could potentially play a role in partially restoring wild-type gene expression.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Remarks to the authors
The submitted manuscript from Faravelli, Rinchetti, Tambalo and colleagues provides a in depth study of SMA underlying disease mechanisms using SMA patient-derived iPSCs to generate spinal cord and cerebral organoids. The team has also leveraged on their established patient-derived spinal cord model to test ASOs based therapeutic strategies, which could rescue both developmental and functional pathophysiological phenotypes.
The team has previously submitted their work to Nature Communications in 2023. Since then, the group has significantly improved the analysis in support of their observations and conclusions, further incrementing the importance of this work. As already discussed, this work importance is supported by several novel aspects:
• Single cell RNA sequencing analysis provides an in-depth characterization of control and SMA derived SCOs indicating developmental dysregulation.
• Generation of SMA cerebral organoids and the study of functional cortical-related dysfunction.
• Electrophysiological analysis is the first of its kind in SMA-derived SCOs and cerebral organoids.
• Evaluation of antisense oligonucleotides efficiency in patient-derived SCOs.
Moreover, the presented revised study expands the mechanistic analysis underlying SMA pathophysiology, investigating downstream splicing defects and therapeutic rescue.
The team has extensively and adequately addressed all remarks provided from this reviewer in the first revision. This has increased the rigor of the scientific approach and significance of the results, which will provide great benefit in the field. I therefore support the publication of this manuscript.
I would like to still mention few minor points, which might require attention or, if addressed, could improve some aspects of the analysis.
Minor points:
Minor point 1
Extended figure 3: figure legend descriptions for sections “c” and “d” have been inverted. Can the author please revise this?
Minor point 2
Figure 2c: I would like to suggest, if possible, to evaluate the ratio of SOX2 reduction between 1 and 2 months in CTRL SCOs and SMA SCOs. This could emphasize the relative lower longitudinal reduction of SOX2 positive cells observed in SMA SCOs. Maybe the author could use grouped stack charts or line chart to better visualize retention of neuronal stem cell state in SMA SCOs.
Minor point 3
Line 197: the sentence “while the altered composition with enriched progenitors and neurons suggests changes in early developmental programs in SMA tissue” could be strengthen by performing statistical analysis of SOX2 positive cells at 2 months between CTRL SCOs and SMA SCOs. This will further support the retention of neural stem cells population and altered developmental programs in SMA. Also, I am not sure if the authors wanted to indicate “enriched neurons” as this seems in contrast with their results.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Most of the comments have been addressed.
It would be reasonable to explain more about the comment "we were unable to assess axon length in neurons derived from cerebral organoids due to technical limitations" to address the question, as the progenitor phenotype is not comparable to the axonal phenotypes.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors are to be commended for their efforts to improve this manuscript. There are extensive data reported and the conclusion that there are early impairments of differentiation of SMA organoids is more convincing. I still have some concerns:
1. There has been a good effort to better characterize the organoids and extended figure 1 and 2 includes some data on 5 CNTLS and 5 SMA. Nonetheless, the number of lines used for the different experiments continues to vary throughout the manuscript and at times is not a sufficient number (n=1-3). There remains no quantification of stem cell or neurodevelopmental markers except for 3 genes in 2 CNTL and 1 SMA line.
The baseline characterization of SMN1/SMN2 gene copy number and SMN protein level remains confusing/weak. IN Ext data FIgure 1e, there is SMN1 and SMN2 qPCR, but is this gene copy number or mRNA? Either way, why would there be detectable SMN1 in the SMA line and why is this not shown for all lines? Ext Data Figure 1F shows mRNA levels I believe, but only display the data as a ratio. It would be ideal to show the mRNA data as absolute values for each FL and delta 7 SMN2 transcripts. If I am reading the manuscript right, there is not western blot data for SMN protein levels in the different CNTL and SMA lines over the organoid differentation period. SMA is caused by reduced SMN PROTEIN expression. It is essential to establish SMN protein levels during th differentation period. The authors discuss the importance of decreasing SMN protein levels during development in SMA in the introduction.
Of note, in extended figure 1d, all the data points for mesoderm, ectoderm, endoderm are at zero-is this a mistake?
2. For Figure 1, single cell data are generated for 2 CNTL and 2 SMA lines. This would ideally be at least 3 individual lines. The figure legend should also make clear which lines were used for this experiment (as has been done for other figure legends). Another point that needs to be discussed as a potential drawback in the discussion is that the single cell analysis is done at a single time point. Trajectory analysis (done later in manuscript) with one time point is not as strong as assessment of more than one time point. Can the authors be certain of developmental impairments based on a single timepoint?
3. Figure 2, high content image analysis is done, but the statistical analysis between CNTL and SMA at each time point should be shown in the figure not just the comparison between 1 and 2 mos within genotype. The SMN protein changes over this interval would be ideal when interpreting these data (See point 1 above). For the apoptosis data, are the TUNEL+ cells definitely neurons? Is it possible that SMA is slower to go through nml developmental pruning?
4. Figure 3, the further trajectory analysis of specific MN clusters looks like a nice addition. An enrichment of MNs along a single branch is observed, but the meaning and implications of this are not discussed in results or discussion. This analysis is based on a single time point and the potential weakness of not assessing more than one time point should be acknowledged in the discussion.
5. I have some concerns about the calcium imaging and am not sure these data are necessary. There is no attempt to assess calcium influx in individual cells and really need to esablish changes in neurons. The electrophysiology data are stronger and make the same point.
6. I appreciate the efforts to improve the ASO treatment experiment. There has been some effort to assess biodistribution with biotin, but all that is included in the manuscript is a single image of biotin ICH that still shown biotin staining predominantly at the periphery. The data supporting efficicent biodistribution should be quantified. It would be ideal to show uptake of ASOs in the motor neurons specifically given this is the most important target cell. Why were 3 doses of ASO required over a fairly short interval? How was the treatment regimen determined?
I am also concerned that there is no inclusion of treated CNTLs in these experiments. This is particularly critical for interpretation of the splicing changes and whether improvements can be definitely attributed to changes in SMN expression. There also seems to be a disconnect between SMN protein induction, which appears fairly modest, and the change in ratio FL/d7 SMN mRNA that ranges from a ratio of 30 to 400? Again seeing the individual FL and d7 mRNA levels would be clarifying.
7. Another important point is that this is not the first published study to report on SMA organoids. See Cell Rep Med 2024 Aug 20;5(8):101659. Isogenic patient-derived organoids reveal early neurodevelopmental defects in spinal muscular atrophy initiation. Tobias Grass et al. I don't see that this paper has been cited or that the findings in the two papers are compared and discussed. This previous publication does potentially lessen the novelty.
Minor:
1) Title may be a bit overstated with rescue of developmental alternations
2) SMA does not show an absence of SMN protein-see line 149 and elsewhere. Better to state SMN is reduced.
3) From abstract, I am not sure I am convinced that the oligo "restored" SMN-would need to show a WB comparing CNTL to SMA treated to prove this.
4) Generic drug nusinersen is lower case and acts on SMN2 pre-RNAs not of SMN2 (italic implying gene).
5) What specific neurofilament was analyzed is unclear. There is mention of SMI32 in text (which assesses both medium and heavy unphosph NF), but the graphic shows NFL and there is NFH in the text. This needs to be clarified
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Review of the single cell analysis: The authors perform single cell analysis in control and SMA iPSC derived spinal cord organoids to study early developmental defects in SMA. The authors demonstrate that gene expression in neuronal progenitors and postmitotic neurons is altered in SMA, suggesting that SMA-related defects start to emerge at very early developmental stages. The authors also note that the developmental trajectory and regulation of motor neurons is altered in SMA. These findings are novel and interesting, however, shortcomings in data analysis and interpretation were noted and are outlined below.
Similarity between single cell sequencing replicates
scRNAseq were performed independently for 2 control and 2 SMA lines. It is stated that data from 27,114 cells were obtained but it is not mentioned how many cells form each genotype and cell line passed the quality control thresholds. In addition, there is no mention of how similar the single cell profiles of the 2 control/SMA lines were to each other . Separate UMAP plots for control and SMA cells are shown in Ext Data Fig. 3a, but within these, it would be important to see the distribution of cells from each of the 2 lines. This is important for understanding line to line variability and ascertain that the differences reported are consistently present in both SMA lines.
Assigning identity to clusters
It is unclear how cells in Fig.1c UMAP are assigned MN identity. Ext. data fig 3e shows module score enrichment for some of the cell types identified but not for MNs. A quick look at the top 300 genes for each cluster in Supplementary Table 4 does not show enrichment of key MN markers in clusters identified as MNs. Specifically, Isl1, Isl2, Mnx1, Aldh1a2, Slc10a4, Arhgap36, which were identified as MN markers in human spinal cord single cell sequencing [PMCID: PMC8353162] seem to be absent in the MN clusters in supplementary table 4. How do the authors explain this? Please include a clear description for how MN identity was assigned to these cell types.
It is understood that cells in organoids will not have the same gene expression pattern as in vivo cells, however it would be useful to know how similar/different the cell types in organoids are to their in vivo counterparts by performing correlation analysis between identified in vitro cell types and in vivo cell types from [PMCID: PMC8353162 and/or PMCID: PMC8567249].
Are MN subclusters differentially affected by SMA?
MNs are treated as one group in the data when quantifying differences in cell population (Fig. 1g). However there seem to be two distinct population of ‘MN’, one expressing Phox2a/b, markers associated with visceral or cranial MNs and another expressing Isl1/Mnx1 which are markers of skeletal MNs including limb innervating. Second, it would be important to quantify these populations separately as they seem to behave differently in control vs. SMA. This seems important because in Fib1f/g, although an overall reduction in MN population is shown, it looks as if one group of MNs (Phox2+) is reduced in SMN SCOs, while the other (Isl1+, Mnx1+) group is increased. Is this the case (based on quantification of cell numbers in these clusters) and if so, how do the authors explain this?

It is clear that there are differences between control and SMA analyses in terms of distribution of cells and regulons, but without an understanding of the biological relevance of these dendograms, it is difficult to conclude that these changes are meaningful for MN development.
Response (Part A – Whole dataset pseudotime): We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We fully agree that applying pseudotime trajectory inference to the entire dataset can lead to overconnected structures that may not reflect true lineage relationships. Specifically, the apparent connection between the motor neuron and V2a/b lineages in the original dendrogram tree is not biologically accurate, as these lineages arise from distinct progenitor domains (pMN and p2, respectively). To avoid overinterpretation of such artifacts, we decided to limit the use of pseudotime in the global analysis. Rather than inferring multi-branching trajectories, we focused on the distribution of pseudotime scores across genotypes and cell types, which provides a robust, model-free readout of transcriptional maturation. The updated version of Figure 2 now shows this analysis. As illustrated in Figure 2f–h, SMA organoids exhibit a significant leftward shift in pseudotime scores compared to CTRLs, consistent with a delay in transcriptional maturation. This trend is observed not only in motor neurons, but across multiple cell types including progenitors, pMN, neurons, V2a/b, and pRP populations. These results support the idea that SMA impacts the overall developmental progression of spinal cord cell types, rather than affecting only a specific lineage. We have revised the text and figure legends accordingly, and we thank the reviewer again for encouraging a more cautious and biologically grounded interpretation of the data.
Response (Part B – MN pseudotime): We thank the reviewer for these thoughtful comments and for pointing out inconsistencies in the original pseudotime trajectory visualization. We have carefully reviewed the analysis and made several corrections and improvements in response:
As the reviewer correctly noted, the original dendrogram contained inconsistencies in color labeling, which may have contributed to confusion regarding cluster identity and trajectory interpretation. We have now corrected these color assignments and added explicit cell type labels to the dendrogram plot to improve clarity.
In revisiting the annotation, we realized that a subset of cells originally labeled as intermediate progenitors (INPs) within the motor neuron (MN) lineage more closely resembled neurogenic progenitors (NPs) based on their transcriptional profile and their comparison to the human fetal reference. We therefore reclassified these cells accordingly and excluded them from the MN partition before re-running the downstream analysis. This refinement improved the biological consistency of the trajectory, as the corrected annotation more accurately reflects known stages of motor neuron development.
With these updates, it is now evident that the region with the highest SOX2 regulon activity, located at the top of the dendrogram, corresponds to the pMN cluster (Figure 3d-e), in agreement with known in vivo developmental patterns. Interestingly, the persistence of SOX2 activity in downstream states, specifically in the SMA condition, may reflect a delay in motor neuron differentiation, as also observed in the global pseudotime analysis (Figure 2f-h). This interpretation is further supported by our immunofluorescence data (Figure 2a-e), which show a sustained presence of SOX2⁺ cells between DIV30 and DIV60 in SMA organoids, in contrast to the decline observed in CTRL samples. We have updated both the Methods and Results sections to clarify that the dendrogram does not represent a strict lineage tree, but rather a continuum of transcriptional states within the MN lineage, shaped by gradual transitions and regulon dynamics. To facilitate interpretation of the heatmaps, we have added top annotations indicating both the pseudotime score (corresponding to the diffusion map shown in Figure 3b) and the cell type/clusters color codes matching the MN subtype labels in Figure 3a. This visual alignment enables the reader to directly relate regulon activity patterns to both transcriptional progression and cell identity.

We have now fully addressed this concern.
The authors should also include a more detailed description of how MN identity is assigned and ideally a comparison of in vitro cells to in vivo MN, V2a, V2b, and progenitors data from human spinal cords.
We have now fully addressed this concern.

The authors summarize these analyses as showing that the development and regulation of progenitor to MN trajectory is disrupted in SMA- while this may be true, the presented analysis does not make a convincing case.
We have now fully addressed this concern.
Immunostaining performed for Sox2 and TuJ1 elsewhere in the manuscript provides some information about the prevelance of progenitor vs. neurons and their developmental/cell death trajectory, but this does not provide specific information about MN trajectory, for which more MN specific markers such as Olig2 (for pMNs), Isl1, Mnx1, Lhx3 (for MNs) would be more useful.
We appreciate the suggestion and recognize the value of further immunostaining analysis. Unfortunately, due to limitations in the remaining material, we were unable to perform additional quantification without initiating a new round of differentiations.

Fig1j and Fig 3g: Unclear which GO terms are from upregulated OR downregulated genes.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
Responses to Reviewer 3:
The authors have largely addressed these comments.
Regarding Q3: Adding additional bar plots is not necessary, but it would be useful to add the comparisons between CTRL and SMA in the form of *, ***, or ns in the plot already presented in Figure 2c, 2d.
Response to Reviewer 4 (review of the single cell analysis):
The authors have carefully considered many of my comments and added extensive new analysis. The additional comparison of single cell data from organoids to in vivo single cell datasets, and the clear subtype labeling of MNs based on marker expression addresses many of my concerns in Q2 and Q3. My concerns in Q4 are also addressed by improvements to the pseudotime/lineage analysis.
However, I’m afraid that my first point (Q1) about how similar single cell profiles within the 2 control/SMA lines are to each other has not been adequately addressed and may actually be a major concern for the interpretation of single cell data.
The individual UMAPs now presented in Supplementary Fig. 3b/c show that there are major inconsistencies within the two CTRL and the two SMA lines. While the authors focus on the inconsistencies between the 2 SMA lines (only one of two lines shows the SMA specific clusters), I am more concerned by the major discrepancy between the two control lines. One of the two control lines (C3) has disproportionately high number of NPs (neurogenic progenitors) and MNs. This is especially pronounced for MNs: in control line 1 (C1), ~15% of sequenced cells are MNs, in contrast, ~60% of cells are MNs in C3. This turns out to be approximately 600 MNs from C1 and 4200 MNs from C3 (based on total cell number provided in Supp. Table 1) that are aggregated together for downstream analysis. Proportions of MNs from SMN lines S1 and S3 are 15% and 35% corresponding to approximately 1200 and 2300 MNs that are aggregated together. I agree with the authors that iPSC lines often show inconsistent differentiation trajectories, but these inconsistencies cannot be ignored in the interpretation of the data:
1. The authors’ claim that MNs are significantly decreased in SMA genotype or that there is a “reduction in MN generation or survival in SMA” is not consistent across lines. If we just compare control line 1 (C1) to either SMA line 1 (S1) or S3, it is not clear that there are fewer MNs in the SMA condition as compared to control. What would the Milo analysis in Figure 1g look like if the authors compared C1 vs S1, C1 vs. S3, C3 vs. S1, and C3 vs. S3. What would it look like if they compared C1 vs. C3. Would the results be consistent with the conclusion that MNs are significantly reduced in SMN compared to control, or would they show that MNs are reduced in all lines compared to C3, which would suggest the difference in aggregated CTRL vs. SMA is simply driven by the unique differentiation trajectory of the C3 iPSC line. Immunostaining for Sox2/Tuj1, while informative, is not sufficient evidence to show that there are fewer MNs in SMA organoids compared to control.
2. The disproportionately high number of fully differentiated MNs in C3 could also skew the pseudotime analysis towards more maturity in aggregated control cells (because the distributions of cells in C3 is uniquely skewed towards the right side of the UMAP in Figure 2f compared to C1, S1, S3). C3 also has many more cells than C1 (7308 vs. 4645) which could further contribute to technical imbalance in the pseudotime analysis. If pseudotime analysis is done on C1 vs. S1, C1 vs. S3, C3 vs. S1, C3 vs. S3, C1 vs. C3 would the results be consistent with the idea that the difference currently shown is SMA dependent?
3. The MNs that are specifically enriched in C3 seem to have a distinct enough gene expression pattern that they make a clearly separate cluster in the aggregated UMAP (bottom cluster of MNs in Fig. 1c, Supp Figure 3b). Lines C1, S1, and S2 do not have a significant number of MNs with this signature. While I agree with the authors that comparing these subtypes to in vivo subtypes is not meaningful, this difference is transcriptional profile is still a concern because it is unclear how if affects the trajectory analysis of MNs in Figure 3. Again, would these analyses give consistent results if C1 vs. S1, C1 vs. S3, C3 vs. S1, and C3 vs. S3 comparisons were performed?
At the very least, the manuscript should mention the discrepancy between the two control lines, and mention that the analysis might be skewed because iPSC line C3 contains disproportionately higher numbers of differentiated MNs which also have a different transcriptional signature. Adding additional line to line (C1 vs. S1, etc) comparisons would be ideal, as it would provide a clearer picture of conclusions that are consistent across lines.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Rebuttal Letter
POINT-BY-POINT RESPONSE TO REVIEWERS
Response to Reviewer 3's comment:
We added the statistical comparisons (*, ***, ns) between CTRL and SMA to Figures 2c and 2d as requested.
Response to Reviewer 4:
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thorough and constructive evaluation of our revised manuscript. We are encouraged that our core findings regarding apoptosis modules, motor neuron-specific signatures, and differential gene expression analysis have been well-received.
We fully acknowledge the reviewer's important concerns regarding cell line variability and its potential impact on our interpretations. In response, we have conducted additional analyses that we believe support our conclusions.
Addressing the consistency of MN reduction across lines (Question 1):
We thank the reviewer for raising the important point regarding the consistency of motor neuron (MN) reduction across individual line comparisons, and for suggesting pairwise testing.
The Milo pipeline builds its statistics on replicates, which allows to increase robustness to sample variability. Because our dataset includes replicates for each individual line, we were able to extend the analysis and run Milo differential abundance testing between all individual lines, thereby directly addressing the reviewer’s suggestion.
In the original analysis (which pooled all lines together), Milo testing supported a reduction of MN-related nodes in SMA compared to controls. The new pairwise analysis (performed by cell line) confirms that both SMA lines contribute to this effect, although in line-dependent directions (Figure below and Extended Data Figure 5). Specifically, one SMA line (S1) shows consistent reductions relative to both controls (C1 and C3), while the other (S3) shows a reduction compared to C3 but a relative increase compared to C1, where MN abundance is already limited. As the reviewer suggested, this heterogeneity likely reflects intrinsic variability among control lines (C1 vs. C3), rather than undermining the overall conclusion of reduced MNs in SMA. Similar variability has also been reported by other groups investigating the reproducibility of different spinal cord spheroid protocols1.
To minimize potential line-driven effects, these analyses could be extended to a larger set of patient-derived lines or complemented with isogenic lines in which specific mutations are corrected. While we acknowledge and reiterate the differences between our model and that of Grass et al.2, as discussed in the previous revision, it is important to note that a reduction in MN abundance was also observed in the isogenic SMA organoids they generated. Importantly, abundance-independent analyses – including pseudotime scoring, pseudobulk differential gene expression, MN trajectory inference, apoptosis module activation, and transcription factor activity (SCENIC) – also converge on a consistent MN-specific defect in SMA compared to controls.
Addressing pseudotime and trajectory concerns (Questions 2 and 3):
The reviewer raised the possibility that higher MN abundance in the control C3 line could bias our developmental/pseuodtime scoring analyses. We wish to clarify that our original analysis was normalized by subsetting the same number of cells per phenotype when comparing pseudotime distributions with the KS test. This approach already ensured fair comparisons and reduced the risk of artificially low p-values, given the sensitivity of the KS test to very large sample sizes. Nevertheless, following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have now further extended the analysis by performing stratified downsampling at the line level (rather than by phenotype) and building pairwise statistics between individual lines. The results were highly consistent with previous findings: every pairwise control–SMA comparison revealed significant developmental delays in SMA, independently from the pairs considered (KS tests: C1–S1, p = 0.015; C1–S3, p = 2.32×10⁻⁹; C3–S1, p = 2.79×10⁻²⁷; C3–S3, p = 2.32×10⁻⁹). Importantly, when restricting the analysis to MNs only – thus removing any influence of differences in cell type composition – the differences in pseudotime scoring remained strongly significant (all p < 0.001) in all comparison, further supporting the aberrant MN differentiation caused by SMA.
Trajectory analyses further confirmed this conclusion. Across all line comparisons, SMA consistently showed the same polarized pattern: an accumulation of cells in progenitor and intermediate states with impaired progression toward terminally differentiated MNs. This effect was reproducible regardless of the control line used as reference and therefore cannot be attributed to C3-specific features. All these new analyses are now implemented in the text and in the supplementary material (Extended Data Figure 9).
Finally, we acknowledge that C3 MNs form a distinct transcriptional cluster, reflecting inter-line variability. Nevertheless, the pathological signatures of SMA – developmental delay, altered trajectories, and apoptotic modules – were reproducible in all comparisons, demonstrating that these are disease mechanisms rather than artifacts of line composition.
Acknowledging limitations and strengthening our conclusions:
We have substantially revised our Discussion section to explicitly acknowledge the variability between iPSC lines. We now clearly state:
"While the developmental phenotype associated with SMA remained consistently detectable and statistically significant, even when analyses were performed within individual genotypes, a limitation of the SCO system is the variability in the representation of different cell populations across genotypes, and some differences in MN abundance between iPSC lines is to be acknowledged, especially in control lines. We recognize that performing analyses on hiPSC lines derived directly from patients offers the advantage of working with patient-specific material, thereby encompassing broader biological variability. As a result, significant findings are more likely to be clinically relevant. On the other hand, the use of isogenic lines would allow a more precise attribution of phenotypic differences to the disease background rather than inter-individual variation, and therefore, this adds a potential limitation to our study."
In conclusion, our additional analyses comprehensively address the reviewer's concerns while strengthening our manuscript. The convergence of evidence from multiple analytical approaches, applied across individual line comparisons, provides robust support for our central thesis that SMA involves fundamental disruptions in neural development that extend beyond simple motor neuron loss. We are grateful for the reviewer's insightful comments, which have prompted us to perform these additional validations that ultimately reinforce the biological significance of our findings.
1. Andersen, J. et al. Generation of Functional Human 3D Cortico-Motor Assembloids. Cell 183, 1913-1929.e26 (2020).
2. Grass, T. et al. Isogenic patient-derived organoids reveal early neurodevelopmental defects in spinal muscular atrophy initiation. Cell Rep Med 5, 101659 (2024).
