## Methods

The studies involving human samples were conducted in accordance with the ethical standards of the Declaration of Helsinki, national legislation, and institutional guidelines. Human fibroblast cell lines were obtained from Eurobiobank with informed consent, as approved by the ethical committee at Fondazione IRCCS Ca’ Granda Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico and University of Milan (0004520).

iPSC reprogramming and culture
Control iPSC lines C1 and C2 were derived from fibroblasts obtained from skin biopsies reprogrammed into iPSCs using the CytoTune iPS 2.0 Kit (CytoTune-iPS Sendai 2.0 Reprogramming Kit, Invitrogen). Control line C3 was obtained from Cedar Sinai CS5NXHiCTR. Control line C4 was obtained from WiCell iPS DF 19-9-11T.H and previously used in Corti et al.62,63. Control line C5 was previously generated from the Corti laboratory and published in Taiana et al.64. SMA line S1 was obtained from Cedars Sinai CS77iSMA. SMA line S2 was obtained from Cedars Sinai CS32iSMA. SMA line S3 was obtained from Cedars Sinai CS83iSMA. SMA line S4 was previously generated from the Corti laboratory65,66. SMA line S5 was previously generated from the Corti laboratory62. All iPSC lines were derived from male donors. IPSCs were maintained in E8 medium (Essential 8™ Medium, Gibco, A1517001) medium at 37°C in 5% CO2.

Embryoid bodies (EBs) formation
Embryoid bodies (EBs) were generated from iPSCs cultured in E8 medium (Essential 8™ Medium (Gibco, A1517001)) at 37°C in 5% CO2. At ~80–85% confluency, iPSC colonies were detached using Collagenase IV at 2 mg/mL (Gibco, 17104019), collected, and gently resuspended in complete EB medium (DMEM/F12 (Gibco, 11320033), KnockOut Serum Replacement (Gibco, 10828028), MEM-NEAA Solution (Gibco, 11140035), 2-mercaptoethanol [55 mM] (Gibco, 21985023), GlutaMAX (Life Technologies, 35050061)) supplemented with bFGF at 4 ng/mL (Peprotech, 100-18B). Cells were transferred to non-treated tissue culture Petri dishes to promote suspension growth. EBs were maintained in suspension for up to 7 days, with medium changes (EB medium without bFGF) every other day following manufacturer’s instructions (Pub. No. MAN0013784 Rev. 1.0).

Generation of cerebral organoids (CrOs)
Cerebral organoids were generated by adapting a previous protocol14. Selected iPSCs were harvested using Accutase (Life Technologies, A1110501) and approximately 9000 iPSCs were plated in each well of an ultra-low attachment 96-well plate (Corning, CLS7007) in pluripotent stem cell media containing low recombinant human FGF-basic (4 ng/ml, Peprotech, 100-18B) and Y-27632 (50 μM ROCK inhibitor Calbiochem, 13624S). On day 6, obtained embryoid bodies (EBs) were transferred to low adhesion 24-well plates (Corning, CLS3473) in neural induction media (NIM) containing DMEM/F12 (Gibco, 11320033), 1% N2 supplement (Gibco, 17502001), 1% GlutaMAX (Life Technologies, 35050061), 1% MEM-NEAA (Gibco, 11140035), and 1 μg/ml heparin (Sigma, H3149). On day 12, the EBs were transferred to droplets of Cultrex® Basement Membrane Matrix Type 2 (BME type 2, Trevigen, 3532-001-02) and grown in differentiation media containing a 1:1 mixture of DMEM/F12 and Neurobasal (Gibco, 21103049) with 0.5% N2 supplement, 1% B27 supplement without vitamin A (Gibco, 12587010), 2-mercaptoethanol, 0.025% insulin (Sigma, I9278), 1% GlutaMAX, and 0.5% MEM-NEAA. After 2 days, the droplets were transferred to a spinning bioreactor containing the same media except for B27 without vitamin A, which was replaced with B27 with vitamin A (Gibco, 17504044). The speed of the spinning bioreactor was gradually increased up to 45 rpm.

Generation of spinal cord organoids (SCOs)
To generate SCOs, the same procedure described for human cerebral organoids was applied from day 0 to day 2. On day 2, half of the medium was changed to fresh medium containing a final concentration of 4 ng/ml bFGF (Peprotech, 100-18B), 50 μM Y-27632 (ROCK inhibitor Calbiochem, 13624S), 3 μM CHIR 99021 (GSK3 inhibitor, Sigma-Aldrich, SML1046), 2 μM SB-431542 (Activin/BMP/TGF-β pathway inhibitor, Sigma-Aldrich, S4317), and 0.2 μM LDN-193189 (inhibitor of the bone morphogenetic protein [BMP] pathway, Stemcell Technologies, 72149). On day 4, the medium was replaced, adding the same small molecules (excluding bFGF and Y-27632). On day 6, the EBs were transferred into ultra-low attachment 24-well plates and cultured in NIM plus 100 nM retinoic acid (RA, Sigma-Aldrich, R3255). On day 12 EBs embedded in Cultrex and cultured with SCO differentiation media (SCODM, composed of 1:1 DMEM/F12 and Neurobasal with 0.5% N2 supplement, 1% B27, 2-mercaptoethanol, 0.025% insulin (Sigma, I9278), 1% GlutaMAX, and 0.5% MEM-NEAA). 1 μM Smoothened Agonist (SAG, Calbiochem, 364590-63-6) was added to the media. On day 14, SCOs were transferred to spinning bioreactors and cultured with SCODM supplemented with RA and SAG. On day 28, concentrations of RA and SAG were reduced to 50% and neurotrophic factors BDNF (Peprotech, 450-02), GDNF (Peprotech, 450-10), and IGF-1 (Sigma-Aldrich, 100-12) were added at 10 ng/ml each.

Immunohistochemistry analysis
Organoids were fixed with 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA) for 15 min at room temperature (RT) and subsequently placed in 30% sucrose/1× PBS overnight at 4°C. The next day, they were embedded in 10%–7.5% gelatin/sucrose, frozen in dry ice, placed at −80°C overnight, and cryosectioned into 20-μm sections using a cryostat. Organoid sections were permeabilized for 1 h in 1× PBS with 0.3% Triton-X (Sigma) and 10% donkey or goat serum (Jackson ImmunoResearch) at RT. 2D cultures were fixed with 4% PFA at RT for 5 min and permeabilized in 1× PBS with 0.2% Triton-X (Sigma) and 10% donkey or goat serum (Jackson ImmunoResearch) for 1 h at RT. Primary antibody diluted in fresh permeabilization solution was added overnight at 4°C (complete list summarized in Supplementary Data 2). The following day, secondary antibodies (Alexa Fluor 488, 555, 568, 594, and 647 conjugates, 1:1000; Invitrogen) were added with DAPI (1:500; Sigma-Aldrich, D9542) in 1× PBS for 90 min at RT. DAKO mounting media (Agilent, S3023) was used to mount the coverslips. TUNEL assay was performed using a DeadEnd™ Fluorometric TUNEL System (Promega, G3250). Confocal images were obtained using a Leica SP8 white laser inverted confocal microscope (Leica) and analyzed using Fiji image-processing software.

Image quantification
To evaluate the number of SOX2+ cells and the percentage of TUJ1-positive area, 10× mosaic images of whole SCOs sections were acquired using an Inverted Microscope DMi8 and the Leica LASX software platform. 20× mosaic images of whole brain organoid sections were imaged using Zeiss Axio Microscope and the Zen Light software platform. At least three different sections were acquired per organoid for at least 3 organoids/cell lines for n > 3 CTRL and SMA lines (Supplementary Data 1). In detail, to compute the number of SOX2+ cells, a custom-written Cell Profiler67 pipeline was designed, and a custom-designed ImageJ/Fiji68 software image macro was applied to evaluate the proportion of TUJ1+ area (as %). For TUNEL quantification, images were acquired by an inverted Nikon-Crest multimodal spinning-disk confocal microscope. Quantification of nuclei (DAPI) and TUNEL-positive cells was performed with an ad-hoc designed analysis pipeline for thresholding and segmentation using the GA2 module in Nis-Elements v5.21 software (Nikon-Lim Instruments). Regarding neurofilament tracing, images previously acquired with a Leica SP8 white laser inverted confocal microscope (Leica) were analyzed using Fiji image-processing software. The NeuronJ plug-in was used for the tracing and analysis of neurite length; only filaments that both originated and terminated within the field of view were traced. Filaments extending beyond the field of view or those for which the origin could not be determined were excluded from consideration.

Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR)
Total RNA was extracted using the ReliaPrep RNA Cell Miniprep System (Promega, Z6010). The RNA concentration was tested using Nanodrop (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Reverse transcription was performed using SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 11756500). 150 ng of template total RNA were retrotranscribed. This protocol has been used to process bulk RNA samples. The expression level of candidate genes (Supplementary Data 3) was assessed by: (i) TaqMan quantitative analysis on the 7500 Real-Time PCR System and 7900HT Fast Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystem), GAPDH was used as a reference gene; (ii) Powertrack SYBR (Thermo Fisher Scientific) quantitative analysis on the ViiA7 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific), ACTB was used as a reference gene.

FL and Δ7 transcript analysis
Total RNA extracted from iPSC or SCOs were retrotranscribed using the SuperScript IV VILO Master Mix (Thermo Fisher Scientific). The relative expression levels of FL and Δ7 transcripts were assessed by RFLP analysis of RT-PCR products (primers available upon request). PCR products underwent o/n digestion at 37°C by DdeI endonuclease, followed by electrophoresis on a 2.5% agarose gel. DdeI recognizes and cuts molecules containing the SMN2 exon 8, allowing the discrimination of the genomic origin (SMN1 or SMN2) of FL and Δ7 isoforms.

Electrophysiology
HD-MEA was used to record the extracellular spontaneous activity of both SCOs and cerebral organoids. The device consists of 4096 planar electrodes measuring 21×21 μm, covering an area of 2.67×2.67 mm (Biocam X with Biochip Arena, 3Brain AG, Switzerland). Organoids were gently positioned on the chip and fixed with a platinum anchor and with a nylon mesh. Before and during recordings, organoids were submerged in Kreb’s solution with the following composition (mM): 120 NaCl, 2 KCl, 1.19 MgSO4, 26 NaHCO3, 1.18 KH2PO4, 11 glucose, 2 CaCl2, oxygenated with a mix of 95% O2/5% CO2 to obtain pH 7.4. Organoids were recorded under control conditions for 15 min, after addition of 100 μM of glutamate (L-glutamic acid, Sigma-Aldrich) for an additional 15 min, and after adding the combination of 100 μM glutamate, 10 μM gabazine (SR-95531, Abcam), and 1 μM strychnine hydrochloride (Sigma-Aldrich) for an additional 15 min. Brainwave X (3Brain AG) software was used to record the electrophysiological activity at the sampling frequency of 17 kHz. Brainwave 4 software (3Brain AG) was used to analyze the traces offline. The precise time spike detection algorithm was used to detect the spikes (parameters used: positive and negative peak, peak duration <1 ms, refractory period >1 ms, and detection threshold >7 times the standard deviation of the noise). Spike sorting was performed using a principal component analysis with K-means (silhouette method) considering a maximum three clusters per electrode and three spikes per cluster. The Pakhira-Bandyopadhyay-Maulik index was used for validating clustering results69. A final check out was performed by the researcher by re-analyzing the signals and removing any confounders. Only channels showing stable activity during the control period (without spike frequency fluctuations exceeding 20% spike frequency) were taken into consideration. The number of channels per organoid considered for the analysis was comparable between control (SCO 13.6 ± 0.6; cerebral 13.8 ± 2.1), SMA (SCO 15.2 ± 0.7; cerebral 15.4 ± 0.9), and treated SMA (SCO 12.8 ± 1.3) organoids. The percentage change in basal firing frequency was calculated by comparing the average firing frequency in the last 10 min before glutamate addition with the interval between 5 and 15 min after glutamate addition.

Morpholino treatment
We used a morpholino (MO-10–34) sequence targeting the SMN2 ISS-N1 region downstream of exon 7 that was previously described by our lab34. The specific MO sequence designed to target SMN2 pre-mRNA was GTAAGATTCACTTTCATAATGCTGG. The CPP used in the study is r6 (RRRRRR, D enantiomeric configuration), which was covalently conjugated to the 5′ end of the MO by our external collaborator, Dr. Hong Moulton. A scramble MO (scr, GTAACATTGACTTTGATATTCCTGG) was used as a control for antisense specificity. We used MO alone and conjugated with r6 peptide (r6-MO)36. As a negative control, we used a custom-made r6-MO containing the scrambled sequence. To assess biodistribution, we used a biotinylated r6-MO that was added to the culture medium as described below. All MO oligomers were synthesized by Gene Tools. We treated SMA SCOs with increasing concentrations of MO or r6-MO. The solution containing 2.4 nmol MO or r6-MO was added directly to each well and incubated for 48 h. Afterward, the culture medium was changed and fresh aliquots of 2.4 nmol MO or r6-MO were added for an additional 48 h. The medium was then replaced with fresh medium for 72 h. Lastly, the organoids were treated again with 4.8 nmol of MO or r6-MO for 48 h.

Western blot analysis
Western blot analysis was performed as described previously34. Briefly, samples were sonicated in lysis buffer supplemented with protease and phosphatase inhibitors (Pierce Rockford, IL, USA) on ice for 10 min. Approximately 25 μg of protein was separated by 12% SDS-PAGE and electrophoretically transferred to a nitrocellulose membrane. The membranes were incubated with anti-SMN (1:1000, BD) and anti-actin (1:1000, Sigma, St. Louis, MO, USA) antibodies. After labeling with peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody (Life Technologies), the proteins were detected using a chemiluminescent substrate (Amersham, Pittsburgh, PA, USA). Signal was detected using LI-COR Odyssey 9120. Densitometry analysis was performed using Image Studio Lite (v5.2).

2D culture of cells from dissociated organoids
SCOs were centrifuged at 300×g for 5 min and trypsin-EDTA was added before transferring the organoids to a 37°C water bath for 5 min. The organoids were then mechanically dissociated, and a double volume of horse serum (Euroclone, ECS0091L) was used to inactivate the trypsin before centrifugation. The supernatant was discarded, and SCO differentiation medium was employed to resuspend the pellet. Approximately 50,000 cells were seeded in 24-well plates with coverslips previously coated with poly-L-ornithine (Sigma-Aldrich, P3655) and laminin (Sigma-Aldrich, L2020). SCODM supplemented with RA, SAG, and growth factors at the same concentration of differentiation day 28, was used for the maintenance of organoid-derived cells.

Whole mount staining
Organoids were washed in 1× PBS and then fixed in 4% PFA on a spinning wheel at 4°C overnight. The following day, five 1× PBS washes (10 min each) were performed on the spinning wheel at RT. Organoids were permeabilized with 0.25% Triton ×-100 in 1× PBS for 15 min. To prevent non-specific binding, organoids were incubated in 1× PBS with 10% FBS and 0.5% serum. Primary antibodies were replaced three times (after 2, 12, and 5 h) and were diluted in 1× PBS with 5% FBS, 0.5% serum of the same species as the primary antibodies, and 0.1% Triton ×-100. Secondary antibodies were diluted in the same solution used for primary antibodies and incubated overnight at RT on the spinning wheel. Images were acquired using a Nikon’s A1R MP+ multiphoton microscope by the Alembic Facility (IRCCS Ospedale San Raffaele).

SCO cell dissociation for single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis
Organoids were dissociated using an optimized protocol based on the Worthington Papain Dissociation System Kit (Worthington Biochemical). Single cell suspensions were collected on ice-cold 1× PBS (without calcium and magnesium) with 0.04% BSA (Sigma-Aldrich) at 1× 10^6/ml as counted by an automatic cell counter (Countess II, Thermo Fisher).

Single-cell RNA-sequencing and downstream analysis
Sample processing. Approximately 8000 cells from each sample, prepared as described above were loaded into one channel of the Single Cell Chip B using the Single Cell 3′ v3 reagent kit (10× Genomics) for gel bead emulsion generation in the Chromium system. Following capture and lysis, cDNA was synthesized and amplified for 14 cycles following the manufacturer’s protocol (10× Genomics). The amplified cDNA (50 ng) was then used for each sample to construct Illumina sequencing libraries. Sequencing was performed on the NextSeq 550 Illumina sequencing platform following the 10× Genomics instructions for read generation. A sequencing depth of ~45,000 reads/cell was obtained for each sample.

Data analysis. Raw sequencing data (bcl-files) were converted to fastq files using the Illumina bcl2fastq tool integrated into the CellRanger (10× Genomics) suite (v3.0.2). The CellRanger analysis pipeline was used to generate a digital gene expression matrix starting from raw data. Reads were aligned to the human GRCh38 reference genome, annotated, and counted with gene annotations from Ensembl version 93. The CellRanger count module was used to map reads with default settings, and the sequence length was set to r1-length=28 and r2-length=55. At least 90,000 reads per cell were produced. For further preprocessing and analysis, we used the Scanpy70 single-cell analysis toolkit (v=1.9.6, pandas v=2.2.0, and numpy v=1.26.3). Doublets were identified and removed with Scrublet71 (v=0.2.3). The threshold at doublet scores was automatically set by the Scrublet algorithm and was used individually for each sample. Quality control metrics, including mitochondrial and ribosomal content, were calculated using sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics function, and then the object was filtered for the outliers cells containing less <10% mitochondrial and <5% ribosomal transcripts. Further, cells were filtered using a sample-specific median absolute deviation (MAD) threshold of “n_genes_by_counts”. After filtering, the data were concatenated using sc.AnnData.concatenate, annotated with sample names and genotypes. We used scVI-tools72 (v=1.1.0) to mitigate batch effects where each genotype and sample was treated as a batch. The AnnData object was first transformed by copying counts to data.layers[“counts”] and identifying 2000 highly variable genes using sc.pp.highly_variable_genes with the Seurat V3 flavor, considering the “Sample” batch key. The transformed data were prepared for scVI analysis by setting up AnnData with categorical covariates “Sample” and “genotype”, and continuous covariates “pct_counts_mt”, “pct_counts_ribo”, and “total_counts”. The scVI model was initialised with scvi.model.SCVI and trained using default parameters. The latent representation was extracted using model.get_latent_representation and stored in adata.obsm[“X_scvi”]. Dimensionality reduction was performed by constructing a KNN graph with sc.pp.neighbors using the latent representation (X_scvi) and running UMAP with min_dist=0.2. Clustering was executed at resolutions 0.25, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, and 1.0 using the Leiden algorithm73 (sc.tl.leiden), and the results were visualized with UMAP plots (sc.pl.umap) displaying cluster assignments, sample information, and genotype. After integration, the data were reverted to all genes using adata.raw.to_adata(). Raw counts were normalized using sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=None, inplace=False) and log-transformed with sc.pp.log1p as suggested in the recent sc-RNA-seq data transformation benchmark study74. The final processed data were saved for downstream analysis. Gene set scores were calculated using Scanpy’s sc.tl.score_genes function. To find DEG, we applied the Wilcoxon rank-sum test on the normalised counts between all found clusters (resolution=0.7), the top 50 genes sorted by the p-value and log-fold change were considered for the biological interpretation.

Differential abundance testing. We performed differential abundance testing using the Python version of Milo25 (v=0.1.1). Neighborhoods were constructed with a proportion of 0.1 using milo.make_nhoods. Neighborhood counts were computed with milo.count_nhoods using the sample column “Sample”. Both genotypes (CTRL and SMA) were encoded as continuous and categorical variables. Differential abundance testing was conducted using milo.DA_nhoods with a design formula based on genotype. A neighborhood graph was built using milopy.utils.build_nhood_graph and visualized with milopl.plot_nhood_graph, highlighting the spatial false discovery rate (FDR) at 1%. Neighborhoods were annotated with cell types using milopy.utils.annotate_nhoods and the color palette from Leiden clustering was mapped to the neighborhoods.

Pseudo-bulk differential gene expression analysis between SCOs genotypes. To test for DEG between genotypes for a particular cell identity (at least 25% of cell proportion for each genotype), we leveraged the PyDESeq275 (v=0.4.4) and the Python implementation of decoupleR76 packages (v=1.6.0). Pseudo-bulk profiles were generated using the decoupler.get_pseudobulk function with a minimum of 10 cells and 1000 counts per group. The pseudo-bulk data were normalized, log-transformed, scaled, and principal component analysis (PCA) was performed. Associations between metadata and principal components were computed using decoupler.get_metadata_associations, and the results were visualized with decoupler.plot_associations. Data were subset by cell type, and differential expression analysis was performed on selected cell types. Genes were filtered by expression with a minimum count of 10 and a minimum total count of 15. The DESeq2 object was constructed with the design factor “genotype” and reference level “CTRL”. Log fold changes (LFCs) were computed, and contrasts between SMA and CTRL genotypes were extracted. DEG were filtered by adjusted p-value (<0.05) and absolute LFC (>0.5). The results then were visualised in the form of complex heatmaps and volcanoplots with custom R scripts. The lists of DEG of selected cell types was analyzed using the Ingenuity Pathway Analysis (IPA—Qiagen Ingenuity Systems) to compute canonical pathways and diseases and functions enrichment.

Prediction of SCOs differentiation states and pseudotime analysis. We performed the prediction of developmental potential on the integrated data using CellRank’s77 (v=2.0.0) implementation of CytoTRACE78. The data were preprocessed by ensuring availability of spliced and unspliced RNA counts, with these layers established from the primary expression matrix when missing. Moments of spliced and unspliced abundances were computed using scvelo.pp.moments. Lately, the CytoTRACE kernel from CellRank was applied to calculate the CytoTRACE score and construct a corresponding transition matrix. CytoTRACE pseudotime was derived from the computed scores to quantitatively represent cellular differentiation status. Pseudotime scores were visualized as density plots comparing different genotypes. Density distributions were estimated using Gaussian kernel density estimation (scipy.stats.gaussian_kde) and plotted as ridgeline plots, color-coded by genotype and cell type. Visualization and figure customization were performed using the Matplotlib library in Python. To statistically compare pseudotime distributions between genotypes (CTRL vs. SMA), a two-sided KS test was performed using SciPy’s ks_2samp function. Pseudotime values for each genotype were extracted, and the KS statistic and associated p-value were computed to assess differences in distribution between groups.

Regulons inference and trajectory analysis of motoneurons lineage. To infer the co-expression modules between transcriptional factors and putative target genes in MN cell lineage, we used the pySCENIC (v=0.12.1) pipeline28. We performed independent pipeline runs for each SCOs genotype data object with the Sungularity container. At the first step of regulons inference, the pipeline relies on a machine learning model that fits the expression patterns of genes to expression patterns of TFs by the GRNBoost279 algorithm. For this part, we used the command line tool (pyscenic:0.12.1 arboreto_with_multiprocessing.py) with the default parameters. Next, the output fits were used to predict the potential regulons and direct-binding targets that are then refined through TFs motif enrichment analysis with (pyscenic:0.12.1 pyscenic ctx) with “–maks dropout” parameter. Lastly, cells were scored for each regulon activity in SMA and CTRL objects, respectively via the AUCell method80 with (pyscenic:0.12.1 pyscenic aucell). Obtained regulons activities scores and metadata were used in the secondary analysis for visualisation and trajectory analysis. We performed trajectory analysis on SCOs focusing on motoneuron linage using Palantir81 (v=1.3.3) and scFates82 (v=1.1.1). The SCOs data object was loaded, and specific clusters unrelated to the MN lineage were removed. Diffusion maps were computed to generate a multiscale diffusion space with four eigenvectors. The principal tree was constructed using scf.tl.tree with parameters method=“ppt”, Nodes=200, ppt_lambda=100, ppt_sigma=sig, ppt_nsteps=200. The root was set to the SOX2 expression using scf.tl.root and corresponded to the pMN. Later, the pseudotime was computed using scf.tl.pseudotime with n_jobs=20, n_map=50, seed=42. To explore the differences in motoneuron differentiation along a shared trajectory, the data were stratified by genotype into CTRL and SMA MN groups. For each group, dendrograms were generated using scf.pl.dendrogram and KDE plots (seaborn.kdeplot). Next, the pySCENIC AUCell output was processed to align with the motoneuron trajectory data generated before and this approach was adopted from the study of Petitpré C et al.83. pySCENIC AUCell output for control and SMA samples was loaded from .loom files. The AUCell matrices were aligned with the trajectory data by matching cell IDs. Regulons active in fewer than six cells were filtered out. Regulon activity was tested for association with trajectory data using scFates and GAM (scf.tl.test_association with n_jobs=20 and A_cut=0.025). Pseudotime for cells was updated based on their order in trajectory analysis (adata.uns[“pseudotime_list”]), and the trajectory model was fitted (scf.tl.fit with n_jobs=20). The trend of specific regulons activity along the trajectory segments was visualised using scf.pl.single_trend and scf.pl.trends. For control samples, a set of significant regulons was highlighted, and the trends of these regulons were plotted. Similar analyses were performed for SMA samples.

Identification of informative splicing gene modules. To associates splicing gene modules to clusters in the SCOs object (CTRL or SMA), we subsetted the object to contain only the selected pools of splicing genes, but all cells. Using scVI dimensionality reduction, Hotspot84 (v=1.1.1) analysis was conducted to identify gene modules by calculating autocorrelations for the genes and identifying significant genes with an FDR < 0.05. Local correlations were computed for the significant genes using 15 parallel jobs, and gene modules were created with a minimum gene threshold of 50, core-only mode, and an FDR threshold of 0.05. Module scores were calculated and assigned to the dataset. Finally, module scores of splicing genes were visualised using scatter plots on UMAP coordinates with custom color palettes.

Stage mapping to reference fetal spinal cord data. To map our control organoid dataset onto a temporal developmental reference, we first processed a fetal spinal cord single-cell atlas23 using Scanpy. After standard cell and gene filtering, the data was normalized, and 2000 highly variable genes (HVGs) were identified using a batch-aware “seurat_v3” approach. We then trained a four-layer scVI model on these HVGs to create a latent reference space. Our control organoid query data was subsequently aligned to this 2000-geneset by adding missing genes with zero expression. Using the scArches (v=0.6.1) package projected the query data onto the reference atlas via partial model retraining. The developmental stage of CTRL organoid cells was then inferred by transferring “Gestational Week” and “Trimester” labels from the atlas using a weighted-kNN classifier (k=100), and we quantified the similarity between query and reference states by calculating cell presence scores.

Cell types mapping to reference fetal spinal cord data. First, the raw count matrix of fetal spinal cord atlas24 was loaded from a .h5ad file into an AnnData object. The raw counts were preserved in a separate layer, after which the data was normalized to a total of 10,000 counts per cell (normalize_total) and subsequently log-transformed (log1p). The top 2000 highly variable genes were identified across batches using the seurat_v3 method on the raw count layer, with the dataset being subset to these genes. To correct for batch effects associated with developmental stages, we employed the scVI-tools package (v=1.3.0). The model was set up using the raw counts and the stage annotation as the batch key. The scVI model was initialized with two hidden layers and trained to learn a latent representation of the cells. This latent space embedding was then used as the basis for semi-automatic annotation. To assign broad cell identities, gene module scores were calculated based on marker genes adapted from ref. 24. These scores enabled the classification of major tissue types, including spinal cord progenitor, spinal cord neuron, sensory neuron/progenitor, mesoderm, hematopoietic, and erythrocytes, as visualized in ref. 24.

Reference model pre-training. A pre-processed and annotated fetal spinal cord dataset was used for scPoli85 model training, a deep generative model designed to integrate datasets from different conditions while preserving cell type identity. We first identified the top 2000 highly variable genes (HVGs) across experimental batches (stage key) using the seurat_v3 method. The scPoli model was initialized on the data subset containing only the HVGs. The model was configured using stage as the condition key and manually assigned cell types as the cell type key. The architecture was defined with a 32-dimensional latent space and a single hidden layer of 1024 nodes. A Zero-Inflated Negative Binomial loss function was used for data reconstruction. The model was trained for a maximum of 50 epochs, with 40 pre-training epochs and an early stopping mechanism which monitored the validation prototype loss with a patience of 10 epochs. Upon completion of training, the learned latent representation was extracted and stored in the original AnnData object. This integrated “X_scpoli” embedding was then used for transfer learning and downstream analysis, including the computation of a k-nearest neighbor graph and visualization with UMAP. To compare our spinal cord organoid dataset with an in vivo reference, we performed computational mapping using a pre-trained scPoli model built on fetal spinal cord atlas. First, the query organoid dataset was loaded, and cells from control (CTRL) samples were isolated for the analysis. To ensure compatibility with the reference model, the query data’s gene set was aligned to the 2000 highly variable genes used to train the reference. Genes present in the reference but absent from the query were added with zero-count expression values. We utilized an scArches86 (v=0.6.1) workflow to project the query data into the reference latent space. The mapping was performed using a partial retraining strategy (retrain=“partial”) for 30 epochs, which fine-tunes the model on the query data while keeping the reference cell embeddings fixed. Following the mapping, we constructed a weighted k-nearest neighbor (wknn) graph in the shared latent space, connecting each query cell to its k=100 nearest neighbors in the reference atlas with HNOCA-tools package87 (v=0.1.1). This graph formed the basis for label transfer, where cell type annotations from the reference were assigned to each organoid cell, yielding the final labels and a quantitative confidence score. The resulting latent space coordinates and transferred annotations were then added back to the original query object for further analysis. Secondly, we calculated cell presence scores for primary tissue to quantify the compositional similarity between the organoid sample and the fetal reference atlas. The resulting latent embedding and annotations were added to the query object for downstream visualization and analysis.

Bulk RNA-seq analyses
Library construction. Libraries were prepared starting from 50 ng of total RNA derived from 9 control, 6 SMA, and 16 morpholino-treated SMA (8 r6-MO, 8 r6-MO-scrambled) organoids, using the SMARTer Stranded RNA-Seq Kit, TaKaRa) and following the manufacturer’s instructions. Samples underwent a high coverage paired-end 150-bp strand-specific sequencing using a NextSeq 2000 platform (Illumina).

Alignment. For each sample (9× control organoids, 6× SMA organoids, 8× SMA organoids treated with r6-MO, and 8× SMA organoids treated with r6-MO-Scramble), raw reads were mapped to the human hg38 genome and counted using STAR v2.7.10a88.

SMN1 and SMN2 counts. SMN1 (SMN-C) and SMN2 (SMN-T) genes are characterized by a very high degree of homology (more than 99%). Thus, to distinguish the reads derived from the two genes, we counted the number of reads mapping to exon 7, where the presence of a nucleotide difference between the two genes enables their unambiguous identification. We performed this check using the IGV tool. Counts mapping elsewhere on the SMN genes were not considered for this analysis.

Differential gene expression analysis. Differential gene expression analysis was carried out using R and the edgeR package v4.0.2 with the functions estimateDisp, glmFit, and glmLRT. Genes having cpm < 0.05 in at least 6 samples were filtered out.

Gene ontology differential expressed genes. Gene ontology of differential expressed genes between CTRL and SMA organoids was done using Ingenuity Pathway Analysis. Terms from “Canonical pathways” and “diseases and functions” were filtered.

Differential splicing analysis. Differential splicing analysis between samples was determined using rMATS turbo v4.3.089, a tool that identifies 5 basic types of AS patterns: SE, MXE, alternative 5′ (A5SS) and 3′ splice sites (A3SS), and retained introns (RI). Significant events were characterized by a FDR < 0.05 and an absolute Inclusion Level Difference > 0.05. Only the reads mapping to exon-exon junctions were used for the analyses. Sashimi plot of events of interest were created using rmats2sashimiplot v2.0.4 (https://github.com/Xinglab/rmats2sashimiplot).

Gene ontology of splicing events. Differential splicing events from SMA vs. CTRL and SMA r6-MO vs. SMA r6-MO-Scrambled were compared. Events sharing (i) the same starting position and the same ending position and (ii) with opposite Inclusion Level Difference were called as “common events”. To annotate gene function, gene ontology was performed using Metascape90. Downstream processing of splicing and gene expression data were done in R v4.1.0 using custom scripts.

Statistical analysis
Continuous variables were reported as mean ± SD. Comparisons between groups and between baseline and post-intervention or interval within a group were assessed using unpaired and paired two-sided Student’s t-test, respectively. One-way or two-way ANOVA was used for comparisons among groups, with Tukey HSD or Sidak’s post-hoc tests applied when the null hypothesis for the omnibus analysis was rejected. GraphPad Prism v.8 was used for all analyses with a significance level of 0.05.

### Reviewer 1

Remarks to the authors.
The study from Faravelli and Rinchetti et al. uses SMA patient-derived iPSCs to generate spinal cord and cerebral organoids to study disease phenotype at early stage of neuronal maturation. Moreover, the authors test the possibility of an antisense oligonucleotide therapeutic strategy to rescue the early disease phenotype in patient-derived spinal cord organoids (SCOs).
This study is not the first to generated SCOs to study SMA [PMID: 30368521], but presents a number of novelties: 1) the single cell RNA sequencing analysis, which provides an in depth characterization of control and SMA derived SCOs at early developmental stages, indicating a possible developmental phenotype; 2) the generation of SMA cerebral organoids and the study of cortical-related dysfunction; 3) the electrophysiological analysis is the first of its kind in SMA-derived SCOs and cerebral organoids; 3) the evaluation of antisense oligonucleotides efficiency in patient-derived SCOs. ### Reviewer 3

In this study, the authors use control and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) spinal cord and cerebral organoids to examine the evolution of gene expression abnormalities over developmental time using single cell sequencing and to assess changes in pre-mRNA splicing patterns after treated with a splice switching antisense oligonucleotide. Emerging data indicate that SMA may start in utero with developmental impairments that are associated with vulnerability to rapid degeneration. Understanding the molecular events underlying these developmental and degenerative events are key for understanding how to optimize therapy.
The major findings of this study are 1) SMA spinal cord organoids may be a useful model of human SMA in vitro 2) there are histological and gene expression signatures suggesting very early developmental slowing involving neuronal and nonneuronal cells and 3) a small proportion of abnormal splicing events improve with ASO treatment. Important strengths of the paper are the effort to develop a human SMA spinal organoid model as prior attempts to look at 2D iPSC derived MNs have not clearly revealed disease relevant pathologies. Further the detailed sequencing of human cells has the potential to reveal new insights into disease pathogenesis. Unfortunately, in its current form, there are several experimental limitations (see below. Although the observation of developmental slowing is interesting, it is not clear whether these findings are relevant for the human disease and there is no mechanistic investigation of the identified gene expression changes to validate their importance.
Specific comments:
1) Several aspects of the initial CNTL and SMA organoid characterizations need to be strengthed. In an extended table, 6 CNTL and 7 SMA lines are listed ranging in age from newborn to 34 years for CNTL and fetal to 2 years for SMA. Only some of these lines are actually used in the paper and for most experiments only 1 to 2 lines each are used. It must be clarified which lines are used for which experiments and whether the differences in subject age play an important role in the behavior of the iPSCs. Further, a minium of 3 lines each (with duplicate derivations) should be used for most experiments. No information regarding SMN1/SMN2 copy number or SMA type is provided. There is no baseline assessment of SMN mRNA or protein levels amongst the different lines over differentiation time (the authors make the point in the intro that SMN may decrease in whole human tissues over developmental time). Although key markers of iPSC differentiation are quantified over differentiation time in several CNTL lines, this quantitative data are not provided for the SMA lines (Ext data figure 1).
2) During the initial characterization of the SMA organoids, the authors note a transcription profile that correlates with Carnegie Stage CS17. They refer to this as a human fetal stage, but in fact this classifcation refers to human embryo staging (first 10 weeks of gestation are embyro and 10-40 weeks are fetus). This is an important distinction as this implies that the organoids are VERY IMMATURE. Although studies of human type I SMA tissues indicate MN developmental abnormalities at mid-late fetal stages, I am not aware of abnormalities dating to the embyro. How do the authors conceptualize the developmental processes in these organoids relative to human SMA development.
3) There seems to be a disconnect between the number of SOX2+ neural progenitors at 1 month and 2 month (CNTL and SMA are equivalent at 2 months) compared to the number of apoptotic cells at these same time points. The authors need to provide the statistical comparison between CNTL and SMA in number of apoptotic cells at 1 mo and 2 months. What cell types are actually dying at 2 months? Do MNs actually undergo apoptotic cells death or is this another cell type?
4) The authors note that there are many gene expression abnormalities between SMA and CNTL, but identify only one gene (NRXN2) that has been previously reported to be altered in SMA tissue. A formal comparison to other data sets might help strengthen the relevance of these gene expression changes.
5) SMI32 is used to define axon length. More thorough analysis to prove these are MNs with MN specific markers and stains that would specifically identify axons vs. dendrites. As is perhaps more accurate to call neurites?
6) Extended data 9 includes only 1 CNTL line (see comment about n above).
7) There is inadequate characterization of the cerebral oraganoids with no quantification of the basic markers over differentation time. Very similar histological and electrophysiological phentoypes are reported in these organoids as reported in the SC organoids. Although the brain may be affected in some very severely affected SMA patients, it is much less severely affected than the spinal cord. It would have been much more impactful to see divergent phenotypes between these two organoid systems-why is this not seen?
9) The treatment experiments as currently presented are not sufficiently rigorous. CNTL lines need to be run in parallel to assess nonspecific changes arising from treatment and as a reference point for SMN expression. A scrambled ASO is also needed. The targeting of the ASO to cells in these organoids need to directly assessed. How many cells and what cell types actually took up the ASO? Were the modest improvements in splicing patterns due to inadequate drug distribution or splicing changes no longer reversible by SMN induction? Those genes that can not reverse their splicing pattern even after full SMN repletion would be very interesting for the SMA field to identify particularly if they are relevant to disease manifestations in patients.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

We thank the Reviewers for their enthusiasm for our work and for their thoughtful comments and constructive feedback for the revisions. We have now addressed all the comments through extensive new data and analyses, as well as text revisions. Here, we first highlight the major changes to the revised manuscript and then address each of the Reviewers' comments point-by-point.
• We have profiled the iPSC lines generated de novo for this publication and specified the features of the commercial and previously published lines. This sums up to 5 iPSC patient and control lines on which most of our analyses have been conducted. This resulted in a new supplementary figure and a new supplementary table (Extended (Ext.) Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1).
• We have generated extensive new data on brain organoids showing a robust functional phenotype, but not a difference in the general amount of SOX2 positive progenitors at the analyzed time point (Fig. 4 and Ext. Data Fig. 9). Our study therefore proposes, for the first time, a direct investigation of brain SMA phenotype and highlights an important difference between brain and spinal cord organoids in the context of SMA pathogenesis.
• As requested, we have increased the number of biological replicates and revised all the immunostaining panels and relative quantification for clarity, adding a color code system to specify which lines were used for each analysis.
• We have also extended our results with numerous new analyses to further support our findings: we added new electrophysiological replicates to all the functional analyses, we updated our single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) datasets with novel computational tools, and we added novel computational analyses for the developmental trajectory and splicing activity.
• We also included novel experiments demonstrating the splicing alternative patterns induced by SMA alterations and rescued by the antisense oligonucleotide treatment. We leveraged a customized scramble sequence to further validate our results, and we repeated all the experiments. In addition, to address the biodistribution pattern of the ASO treatment, we employed a customized biotinylated ASO sequence and verified the extent of the treatment distribution in spinal cord organoids.
Overall, with the addition of these data and analyses, we are confident that we have addressed all the points raised by the Reviewers. These data further reinforce our conclusions on progenitor involvement in the pathology and the pervasive cellular response to a clinically meaningful molecular treatment.

In this study, Faravelli et al compared human SMA type 1 “spinal cord organoids” and “cerebral organoids” from multiple donors. Single-cell RNA-seq revealed changes in the gene expression in various cell types, not only in motor neurons. These included neural progenitors and showed pathological changes in neuronal differentiation. Multi-electrode array analysis showed abnormalities in the activity of both SMA spinal and cerebral organoids. This suggests that SMA pathogenesis could be widespread throughout the central nervous system. The use of antisense oligonucleotides targeting SMN expression in the early stages of organoid development showed a rescue of both morphological and functional deficits in SMA spinal cord organoids. Erroneous splicing in SMN1-target mRNAs was corrected by early treatment.
Overall the manuscript provides important insights into early pathogenesis mechanisms of SMA, which could not be easily assessed without using human iPS cell-derived neural organoids. The comparison between “spinal cord” and “cerebral” organoids highlighting similarities and differences in disease-induced alterations, as well as the demonstration of treatment mechanisms at cellular and molecular levels, are indeed novel valuable contributions to the field. The suggestions to strengthen the study design and the depth of the analysis were valuable and have improved our manuscript. Below, we detail our point-by-point response to each suggestion, and we believe we have comprehensively addressed the Reviewer’s concerns, providing further support for our results, and highlighting the overall value of the study.
Comment
The “spinal cord organoids” are characterized by immnunostaining and scRNAseq. Please compare percent of key cell types (motorneurons, inhibitory neurons, excitatory neurons, progenitors, glia etc) observed by immnunostaning and scRNAseq so that the cellular composition of the organoids. Comparison of the cellular composition between spinal cord organoids and cerebral organoids is critical as basis for the overall study. Please include HB9 for identification of motor neurons.
We wish to thank the Reviewer for their kind remarks regarding the significance of our work in the field of SMA. In response to their comments, we have conducted additional analyses using both immunostaining and scRNA-seq data to provide a comprehensive characterization of the cellular composition of spinal cord organoids and facilitate a robust comparison with cerebral organoids.
To specifically address the identification of motor neurons, we included HB9 immunostaining using a customized and validated antibody obtained in collaboration with the Motor Neuron Center at Columbia University. Additionally, we performed longitudinal immunostaining for SOX2 (progenitor marker) and TUJ1 (neuronal marker). To improve the robustness of these analyses, we increased the number of replicates and provided novel high-resolution immunostaining panels in the revised manuscript. These updates further highlight key differences between CTRL and SMA spinal cord organoids. Specifically, CTRL organoids exhibited a clear reduction in SOX2-expressing neural progenitors and an increase in TUJ1-positive post-mitotic neurons between 1 and 2 months, while SMA organoids showed a less pronounced reduction in SOX2 levels and no significant increase in TUJ1-expressing cells, reflecting a developmental delay.
For cerebral organoids, we specifically assessed whether neural progenitors are affected in SMA by quantifying SOX2+ cells. Our results revealed no significant differences in SOX2+ cell populations between CTRL and SMA cerebral organoids. This finding supports a milder phenotype in the brain compared to the spinal cord, consistent with the known pathogenesis of SMA, where the spinal cord is typically more severely impacted.
ScRNA-seq analysis further validated these findings by revealing distinct cellular trajectories in the 2-month dataset. Cells in CTRL spinal cord organoids split into two primary branches: one comprising progenitors in different proliferative states and committed progenitors of the floor plate, and the other comprising progenitors differentiating into mature neuronal subtypes. In SMA spinal cord organoids, the distribution of cell states was significantly altered, with an increased representation of cells at earlier developmental stages and a statistically significant reduction in cells reaching the endpoint of the trajectory, corresponding to mature neurons (revised Fig. 2f-g).
To ensure robust comparisons of cellular composition, we reanalyzed the scRNA-seq data using the latest computational pipelines, allowing for a more accurate characterization of transcriptional differences. This included a detailed analysis of unmatched SMA cells and a partitioning of the scRNA-seq dataset to examine motor neuron lineages across pseudotime and differentiation stages. These additional insights, now included in the revised manuscript (new Fig. 3), strengthen the foundation of our study and provide a more comprehensive understanding of the cellular differences between SMA and CTRL organoids.
Retinoic acid-induced ventralization could reduce other types of cells in the organoids. Please discuss how retinoid acid-mediated differentiation was controlled in the spinal organoids. Figure 4a indicates SAG and RA are always added to the culture media. Was this intended to maximize motor neuron differentiation and maintenance?
To achieve a spinal organoid model with a high proportion of motor neurons, we employed a combination of retinoic acid (RA) and Smoothened Agonist (SAG). This approach was specifically designed to impart a rostral spinal cord identity to the organoids while simultaneously promoting ventralization, which is essential for motor neuron specification. The consistent addition of RA and SAG to the culture media was intended to maximize motor neuron differentiation and maintenance.
While this protocol prioritizes motor neuron production, it also supports the differentiation of spinal cord interneurons, providing a more comprehensive spinal cord-like cellular diversity. To mitigate potential over-ventralization effects, we carefully optimized the concentrations and timing of RA and SAG addition to achieve a balanced cellular composition.
Our approach aligns with the conditions described in Andersen et al., 2020 (PMID: 33333020), particularly those outlined in conditions 11 and 12, where similar concentrations of RA and SAG were used to drive motor neuron differentiation while preserving cellular diversity within spinal organoids.
Figure 3d indicated reduction of axon length in SMA neurons from spinal cord organoids. Was this similar in neurons from cerebral organoids?
We thank the Reviewer for this insightful question. While we were unable to assess axon length in neurons derived from cerebral organoids due to technical limitations, we instead focused on the assessment of neural progenitors in cerebral organoids to provide a comparative phenotype. This allowed us to explore potential differences between spinal cord and cerebral organoids in the context of SMA.
Please explain the y-axis of Figure 4d in more detail. Was it “increased” percentage from the base line? Was it measured right after adding glutamate directly onto the organoids? Please also provide representative traces and raster plots. Also was Extended Figure 10i analyzed at similar time point with Figure 4d? Representative traces should be presented to know temporal changes. as active number of electrodes different between SMA, control organoids, and MO-treated SMA organoids?
We thank the Reviewer for these important comments, which allowed us to further refine and enhance the robustness of our functional analyses, a key point of novelty in this manuscript. The y-axis of Fig. 4d represents the percentage change in basal firing frequency. This was calculated by comparing the average firing frequency in the last 10 minutes before glutamate addition with the interval between 5-15 minutes after glutamate addition. This information has now been clearly specified in the Methods section.
To provide a more comprehensive view, we have added raster plots for the four conditions (CTRL and SMA, before and after glutamate) to the panel, alongside representative traces. These additions offer better visualization of temporal changes in neuronal activity. Importantly, the number of electrodes considered for the analysis was consistent across all three groups (CTRL, SMA, and MO-treated SMA organoids), and this has been explicitly noted in the Methods.
Regarding the timing of the analyses, we confirm that Ext. Data Fig. 9f (previously named Ext. Fig. 10i) was assessed at a similar time point as Fig. 4c (previously named Fig. 4d), ensuring comparability. Additionally, we have increased the number of replicates for the functional analyses and included a color-coded assignment for each genetic background to increase clarity and reproducibility.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study, the authors use control and spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) spinal cord and cerebral organoids to examine the evolution of gene expression abnormalities over developmental time using single cell sequencing and to assess changes in pre-mRNA splicing patterns after treated with a splice switching antisense oligonucleotide. Emerging data indicate that SMA may start in utero with developmental impairments that are associated with vulnerability to rapid degeneration. Understanding the molecular events underlying these developmental and degenerative events are key for understanding how to optimize therapy.
The major findings of this study are 1) SMA spinal cord organoids may be a useful model of human SMA in vitro 2) there are histological and gene expression signatures suggesting very early developmental slowing involving neuronal and nonneuronal cells and 3) a small proportion of abnormal splicing events improve with ASO treatment. Important strengths of the paper are the effort to develop a human SMA spinal organoid model as prior attempts to look at 2D iPSC derived MNs have not clearly revealed disease relevant pathologies. Further the detailed sequencing of human cells has the potential to reveal new insights into disease pathogenesis. Unfortunately, in its current form, there are several experimental limitations (see below. Although the observation of developmental slowing is interesting, it is not clear whether these findings are relevant for the human disease and there is no mechanistic investigation of the identified gene expression changes to validate their importance.
We are grateful to Reviewer #3 for recognizing the significant strengths of our work and its potential implications for advancing the understanding of SMA pathology. We also deeply value the constructive suggestions to refine our study design, which have enabled us to draw more robust and accurate conclusions. In response to their feedback, we have thoroughly addressed each concern and believe that these improvements have substantially enhanced the rigor and impact of our study.
Specific comments:
1) Several aspects of the initial CNTL and SMA organoid characterizations need to be strengthed. In an extended table, 6 CNTL and 7 SMA lines are listed ranging in age from newborn to 34 years for CNTL and fetal to 2 years for SMA. Only some of these lines are actually used in the paper and for most experiments only 1 to 2 lines each are used. It must be clarified which lines are used for which experiments and whether the differences in subject age play an important role in the behavior of the iPSCs. Further, a minium of 3 lines each (with duplicate derivations) should be used for most experiments. No information regarding SMN1/SMN2 copy number or SMA type is provided. There is no baseline assessment of SMN mRNA or protein levels amongst the different lines over differentiation time (the authors make the point in the intro that SMN may decrease in whole human tissues over developmental time). Although key markers of iPSC differentiation are quantified over differentiation time in several CNTL lines, this quantitative data are not provided for the SMA lines (Ext data figure 1).
In the current version of the manuscript, we addressed all the points raised here by the Reviewer, further strengthening the robustness of our results.
We increased the number of lines for the experiments and made clearer their allocation in the different analyses (we provide a novel Supplementary Table 1 where all experiments are clarified, and we maintained a color code for each line throughout the entire manuscript). This implied the generation of new batches of both spinal cord and brain organoids from CTRL and SMA lines. We have now provided color-coded graphs where organoids have been annotated by the cell line of origin. As it can be observed, several replicates and multiple cell lines have been analyzed throughout all the analyses with negligible inter-line effect. For this revision, we increased the number of replicates and batches for each line, as highlighted both in the newly generated Supplementary Table 1 and across all figures in the manuscript.
For SMN1/2 copy number, we have now provided an extensive characterization of all the iPSC lines generated de novo for this work, including evaluation of 1) morphology, 2) genome integrity, and 3) self-renewal markers (newly generated Ext. Data Fig. 1). We used the same parameters on representative commercial lines, as internal controls. Regarding the commercial and previously published lines, we provided more detailed information about their source and features.
Finally, we extensively characterized the SMN molecular phenotype of the iPSC lines (such as qPCR analyses on the copies of SMN and the evaluation of the expression of the ratio FL/D7 SMN and SMN expression levels over time in culture, Ext. Data Fig. 1d-f) and provided further details of the clinical phenotypes of each donor/patient (Ext. Data Fig. 1h).
Key markers of iPSC differentiation have been quantified over in SMA lines as well in the revised version of the manuscript (Ext. Data Fig. 1g).
2) During the initial characterization of the SMA organoids, the authors note a transcription profile that correlates with Carnegie Stage CS17. They refer to this as a human fetal stage, but in fact this classifcation refers to human embryo staging (first 10 weeks of gestation are embyro and 10-40 weeks are fetus). This is an important distinction as this implies that the organoids are VERY IMMATURE. Although studies of human type I SMA tissues indicate MN developmental abnormalities at mid-late fetal stages, I am not aware of abnormalities dating to the embyro. How do the authors conceptualize the developmental processes in these organoids relative to human SMA development.
We thank the Reviewer for raising this important point and apologize for any lack of clarity in the original submission. In the revised manuscript, we updated our references for the endogenous tissue (Ext. Data Fig. 3c) to include a study that performed single-cell RNA sequencing of human spinal cord cells across multiple time points during embryonic and fetal stages. Our dataset showed the strongest alignment with early developmental stages (first trimester), and we have amended our text accordingly. The transcriptional alterations observed in progenitors, which represent a significant novelty, align with the developmental nature of the model and provide valuable insights into the early events of human spinal cord neurogenesis.
3) There seems to be a disconnect between the number of SOX2+ neural progenitors at 1 month and 2 month (CNTL and SMA are equivalent at 2 months) compared to the number of apoptotic cells at these same time points. The authors need to provide the statistical comparison between CNTL and SMA in number of apoptotic cells at 1 mo and 2 months. What cell types are actually dying at 2 months? Do MNs actually undergo apoptotic cells death or is this another cell type?
We thank the Reviewer for the opportunity to clarify these points. While CTRL SCOs exhibited a clear reduction in SOX2-expressing neural progenitors and an increase in the post-mitotic neuronal marker TUJ1 from 1 to 2 months, SMA SCOs demonstrated a less pronounced reduction in SOX2 levels and no significant increase in the proportion of TUJ1-expressing cells. Single-cell trajectory analysis of the 2-month dataset revealed two major branches: one containing progenitors in distinct states of proliferative activity and committed progenitors of the floor plate, and another comprising neural progenitors progressing toward differentiated neurons (revised Fig. 2f-g). SMA SCOs displayed a strikingly altered distribution of cell states, with an increased representation of cells at the starting and early segments of the developmental trajectory—indicative of an intermediate stage of development. This altered trajectory was accompanied by a robust and statistically significant reduction in cells at the endpoint of the trajectory, corresponding to maturing neuronal subtypes.
We appreciate the Reviewer’s suggestion to conduct further analyses to confirm cell death processes. Although we attempted supplementary staining using markers such as caspase-3, these efforts did not yield reliable results. Additionally, technical limitations—commonly encountered in 3D organoid models due to the extracellular matrix— made it challenging to perform double staining of TUNEL with other markers. The harsh conditions required for the TUNEL protocol interfered with other staining procedures. We have acknowledged this limitation in the manuscript and tempered our conclusions regarding cell death accordingly.
To address this challenge, we leveraged single-cell data to investigate the enrichment of apoptotic genes. Our analyses revealed that the motor neuron cluster exhibited the highest enrichment for apoptotic gene ontology terms among the relevant clusters (Ext. Data Fig. 5c). This observation, combined with the altered developmental trajectory in SMA SCOs, suggests that the vulnerability of motor neurons to apoptosis could be linked to their disrupted progression through differentiation.
4) The authors note that there are many gene expression abnormalities between SMA and CNTL, but identify only one gene (NRXN2) that has been previously reported to be altered in SMA tissue. A formal comparison to other data sets might help strengthen the relevance of these gene expression changes.
After reanalyzing our data using the latest scRNA-seq pipeline, we obtained a cleaner and more robust dataset. We performed a de novo comparison of bulk RNA-seq data from in vitro differentiated SMA and CTRL human motor neurons (PMID: 30649277) with the scRNA-seq differentially expressed genes (DEGs) identified in motor neurons. This updated analysis yielded an expanded list of previously reported genes, now totaling 24. These include CAMK2B, GRIA1, GRM4, NRXN1, PCDH7, PCDH10, PRKCG, PSD2, SCN2A, and SNAP91, many of which are associated with neuronal function and ion channel activity.
5) SMI32 is used to define axon length. More thorough analysis to prove these are MNs with MN specific markers and stains that would specifically identify axons vs. dendrites. As is perhaps more accurate to call neurites?
We agree with the Reviewer and have amended the text and figure legend accordingly.
6) Extended data 9 includes only 1 CNTL line (see comment about n above).
The Reviewer is correct in pointing out this limitation. In the current version of the manuscript, we have highlighted the contribution of each cell line to the respective analyses. While we were unable to increase replicates across all experiments for the brain organoids due to cost and time constraints, we prioritized increasing the number of lines, batches, and replicates for the key experiments. This ensured alignment with the approach used for the spinal cord organoids. Specifically, for the functional analyses, this effort resulted in the production and analysis of additional organoids for the MEA glutamate assay (Fig. 4h, i).
7) There is inadequate characterization of the cerebral organoids with no quantification of the basic markers over differentation time.
Brain organoids are inherently heterogeneous, and we specifically selected this model to provide an unbiased assessment of the potential impact of SMA on the CNS. This approach allowed us to investigate the broad effects of SMA without limiting our analysis to specific brain regions, thereby supporting the overarching hypothesis of our study. While this heterogeneity adds value by capturing a more comprehensive view of SMA pathology, it also presents challenges in organoid-to-organoid reproducibility.
To address this, we focused our quantitative analyses on the general progenitor marker SOX2, assessing its expression at both the protein and RNA levels. This decision aligns with our findings in spinal cord organoids, which represent a central focus of the manuscript. Furthermore, we characterized the emergence of specific neural markers at selected time points to provide additional insights into the differentiation timeline and cellular composition of the organoids.
Very similar histological and electrophysiological phentoypes are reported in these organoids as reported in the SC organoids. Although the brain may be affected in some very severely affected SMA patients, it is much less severely affected than the spinal cord. It would have been much more impactful to see divergent phenotypes between these two organoid systems-why is this not seen?
We appreciate the Reviewer’s observation regarding the phenotypic similarities between the cerebral and spinal cord organoids and the suggestion that divergent phenotypes would be more impactful. To address this, we expanded our analysis on cerebral organoids, focusing on the characterization of fundamental markers and, in particular, progenitor cell phenotypes.
Specifically, we assessed whether neural progenitors are affected in SMA cerebral organoids by quantifying SOX2+ cells. Our results revealed no significant differences in SOX2+ cell populations between CTRL and SMA cerebral organoids. This finding supports the Reviewer’s suggestion of a milder phenotype in the brain compared to the spinal cord, consistent with the known pathogenesis of SMA, where the spinal cord is typically more severely impacted.
9) The treatment experiments as currently presented are not sufficiently rigorous. CNTL lines need to be run in parallel to assess nonspecific changes arising from treatment and as a reference point for SMN expression. A scrambled ASO is also needed. The targeting of the ASO to cells in these organoids need to directly assessed. How many cells and what cell types actually took up the ASO? Were the modest improvements in splicing patterns due to inadequate drug distribution or splicing changes no longer reversible by SMN induction? Those genes that can not reverse their splicing pattern even after full SMN repletion would be very interesting for the SMA field to identify particularly if they are relevant to disease manifestations in patients.
We thank the Reviewer for highlighting this important aspect. During the revisions, we conducted additional batches of SCOs and implemented a robust experimental design to address the concerns raised. Treatments with r6-MO, scrambled r6-MO, and collections of untreated SMA SCOs were performed in parallel, allowing us to assess nonspecific changes and establish an appropriate reference point, as suggested by the Reviewer. The use of scrambled r6-MO as a control provided a stringent analytical framework, ensuring that the observed changes were specific to r6-MO treatment. This approach enabled the identification of a robust set of key genes whose splicing was reverted upon r6-MO treatment (revised Fig. 6). Importantly, genes that did not exhibit splicing reversion were linked to broader pathophysiological processes, suggesting systemic involvement beyond spinal cord pathology (new Suppl. Table 10).
To address the distribution of r6-MO within the organoids, we utilized a biotinylated version of r6-MO and traced its localization using biotin staining (Ext. Data Fig. 10d). The staining revealed widespread distribution of r6-MO, spanning both the periphery and the center of the organoids. This widespread distribution, coupled with the recovery of SMN levels (Ext. Data Figure 10e), suggests that the modest splicing improvements observed are likely related to the irreversible splicing state of certain genes. Interestingly, among the genes associated with reverted splicing events, we identified histone-modifying enzymes, which could potentially play a role in partially restoring wild-type gene expression.
